articles.body:
El órgano electoral revoca una decisión de la Junta Provincial y resuelve que la presidenta, que responsabilizó presidente de supuestos “actos violentos” de los acampados, pudo vulnerar la LOREG

La Junta Electoral Central ha dado la razón al PSOE en su denuncia a la presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid al respecto de un vídeo con una declaración institucional de Isabel Díaz Ayuso tras el desalojo de la acampada pro derecho a la vivienda de la Puerta del Sol en la que la dirigente criticaba con dureza al presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, y llegaba a culparlo de supuestos “actos violentos” de los acampados. El PSOE denunció las palabras de Ayuso, difundidas en sus redes y las de la Comunidad, ante la Junta Electoral Provincial de Madrid, pero esta lo desestimó. Ahora la JEC revoca esa decisión, estima el recurso de los socialistas y resuelve abrir expediente contra Ayuso.

En el vídeo objeto de la denuncia, Ayuso responsabilizaba a Pedro Sánchez y a Francisco Martín Aguirre, ya entonces exdelegado del Gobierno en Madrid, de lo ocurrido en la Puerta del Sol. En el vídeo, una declaración institucional, la dirigente popular afirmó que el legado del sanchismo era “ilegalidad, caos, abandono, suciedad, violencia y miseria”, unas expresiones que la JEC califica ahora de “manifiestamente peyorativas” y que, considera, excedían la información necesaria para explicar el desalojo de la céntrica plaza madrileña.

Ayuso atribuyó directamente a Sánchez la responsabilidad por la acampada, nacida de las protestas por el desalojo de la octogenaria Maricarmen Abascal (que falleció días más tarde en un hospital): “Pedro Sánchez ha permitido otra vez una situación ilegal que se ha producido en Madrid durante 38 días”. Según la popular, el presidente del Gobierno “consintió por interés político que se ocupara ilegalmente” Sol. “Sánchez y su delegado en Madrid hasta hace una semana son culpables, responsables del secuestro de este lugar público, de los actos violentos que se han llevado a cabo durante todos estos días, 38 días, en esta plaza y en toda la zona, también de la vandalización del patrimonio de todos”, afirmaba Ayuso.

La presidenta consideró que era responsabilidad del presidente del Gobierno que se hubiera puesto “en peligro la sede de presidencia de la Comunidad de Madrid, la Real Casa de Correos, y también impedir su normal funcionamiento”. No quedaban ahí las atribuciones de culpas: Sánchez era el responsable de una “ruina (...) a todo el comercio de la zona, a personas inocentes que incluso han tenido que despedir a empleados”, afirmó literalmente, lo que causó, según la dirigente, unas pérdidas “que superan los 30 millones de euros”.

En contraste con esa andanada contra Sánchez, en el mismo vídeo Ayuso daba las gracias a la nueva delegada del Gobierno, las fuerzas y cuerpos de seguridad del Estado, la Policía Municipal y a los servicios públicos del Ayuntamiento, en particular a los de limpieza, que, dijo, retiraron “en tiempo récord toneladas de basura y suciedad que han acumulado los acampados para vergüenza de todos”.

Ahora, en su razonamiento para expedientar a Ayuso, la Junta entiende que queda fuera de duda que las palabras de la presidenta contra Sánchez afectan al principio de neutralidad. La JEC entiende que las declaraciones y su difusión en redes sociales pueden atentar contra el artículo 50.2 de la LOREG, que prohíbe a los poderes públicos, en periodo electoral, aludir a los logros de gestión y usar imágenes o expresiones similares a las de los partidos.

Ayuso alegó ante la JEC que el PSOE omitía en su denuncia que el vídeo se retiró de las redes sociales de la presidenta y de la Comunidad de Madrid donde se había emitido. La dirigente popular esgrimía también que la declaración institucional se produjo en el marco de un asunto que afectaba directamente a la Comunidad de Madrid. Y rechazaba tanto que el vídeo incorporase expresiones propias de un partido que se presenta a las elecciones del 29 de noviembre —algo vetado por la LOREG— como que su actitud contra el presidente fuera “recurrente”. Tras la retirada del vídeo de marras, la JEC deja para el procedimiento sancionador abierto la valoración de esa reincidencia que ha alegado el PSOE.

articles.title: Why are winter rains forcing Palestinians in Gaza to flee again?
articles.summary: Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid, damaged buildings and flooded tents leave displaced Palestinians vulnerable.
articles.preview: Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid, damaged buildings and flooded tents leave displaced Palestinians vulnerable. When heavy rain swept through az-Zawayda in central Gaza in early November, water rushed into Jaber al-Kaseeh’s tent, soaking his family’s mattresses and spoiling their food. Al-Kaseeh, who fled Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, told Al Jazeera that his camp had flooded three or four times the previous winter. Those floods had already driven many of his neighbours away.
articles.body:
Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid, damaged buildings and flooded tents leave displaced Palestinians vulnerable.

When heavy rain swept through az-Zawayda in central Gaza in early November, water rushed into Jaber al-Kaseeh’s tent, soaking his family’s mattresses and spoiling their food.

Al-Kaseeh, who fled Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, told Al Jazeera that his camp had flooded three or four times the previous winter. Those floods had already driven many of his neighbours away.

About 1.36 million Palestinians, 65 percent of Gaza’s population, are living in tents and makeshift shelters, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).

The storm that began on the evening of November 6 flooded about 70,000 tents within 12 hours, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. Preliminary UN estimates suggest it affected about 226,000 people, including more than 5,000 households left sleeping without shelter. About 600 households were forced to move again.

The rain also killed people. On November 8, a sand embankment collapsed onto tents at a displacement camp south of Deir el-Balah, killing five people, including children. OCHA reported that an infant drowned during the same storm and a nine-month-old baby died of hypothermia on November 13.

The Union of Gaza Strip Municipalities warned on Wednesday that about 1,000 camps and other shelter sites could flood this winter. The councils say 200,000 worn-out tents need replacing and more than 2,000 damaged buildings are at risk of collapse.

As Gaza enters its fourth winter since Israel launched its genocidal war in October 2023, we look at how Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid, damaged buildings and flooded tents leave displaced Palestinians at greater risk.

Why can’t Palestinians move somewhere safer?

Israeli restrictions keep Palestinians from reaching large parts of Gaza, which leaves them fewer options to move to safer areas, according to OCHA. On November 17, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the World Food Programme said Gaza’s population had been confined to less than 40 percent of the territory and that more than half of its 1,700 displacement sites were on flood-prone land.

The threat of further displacement persists. On Thursday, Israel Katz, the defence minister in Israel’s caretaker government, threatened a new offensive that would move one million Palestinians south if Hamas did not disarm. Writing on X, he called Hamas’s control over the remaining 30 percent of Gaza “an illusion”. He did not issue an evacuation order.

Damaged homes offer little refuge. About 82 percent of Gaza’s structures had been damaged or destroyed by mid-June, according to UN satellite analysis.

In Nuseirat, Nasser al-Hajj took his children to a neighbour’s home during the first November storm as debris fell from the ceiling of his flat, which an Israeli attack had damaged. “But where am I supposed to go? Rent is expensive, and a tent is not safe either,” he told Al Jazeera.

Why is Gaza so vulnerable to flooding?

Israel’s war has wrecked the drains and sewers that would normally carry rainwater away. In Gaza City, eight pumping stations and three main rainwater collection basins were out of service when the first storm hit, municipal spokesperson Hosni Muhanna said. Even under the best conditions, he said, the remaining network could handle no more than a fifth of the rainwater.

At Sheikh Radwan lagoon, one of the city’s main collection basins, the water rose by nearly 1.5 metres (five feet) during the storm, OCHA reported. Its pumping station is operating at less than 40 percent of its design capacity, the UN office added on Thursday.

In central Gaza, the councils are worried about water rising suddenly in Wadi Gaza and flooding al-Mughraqa and az-Zahra. Emergency services are overstretched: Gaza’s civil defence said it received 2,166 distress calls on November 7 but could send crews to only 218; most callers received advice by phone.

What are the health risks?

During the early November rains, the UN said crews used suction trucks to remove water mixed with sewage from 58 shelters. At the Patient’s Friends Benevolent Society Hospital in Gaza City, water flooded the basement that housed the children’s department, pharmacy and radiology services. Elsewhere, flooded roads kept patients and staff from reaching clinics.

Crowding poses a separate risk. Families in crowded tents have too little water to maintain basic hygiene, paediatrician Sharif Matar told Al Jazeera at Gaza City’s Rantisi Children’s Hospital.

The World Health Organization (WHO) recorded 692 suspected meningitis cases between October 1 and November 23, most of them among babies under a year old. Gaza’s Ministry of Health issued an epidemic alert on November 24 after recording 272 cases in October, compared with a usual monthly average of 30 to 50.

Why isn’t enough shelter aid reaching families?

On November 13, the UN’s humanitarian team said more than 150,000 tents bought by aid organisations and governments were waiting outside Gaza, most of them in Egypt’s El Arish. On Wednesday, the European Commission said tents were still waiting on trucks because Israel had not allowed them or the equipment needed to put them up to enter. Goods from Egypt are routed for inspection through the Karem Abu Salem crossing (called Kerem Shalom in Israel) rather than entering directly through Rafah. Israeli authorities also classify some shelter supplies as “dual-use”, which limits how much aid groups can bring in.

COGAT, the Israeli military body that coordinates aid, said on Monday that nearly 100,000 tents had entered Gaza under its winter programme. It said it had approved more than 67,000 tents and other winter supplies that had yet to be brought in. Inside Gaza, shelter agencies have fewer than 6,500 tents in stock, the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) said on Wednesday.

Restrictions and shortages have pushed up prices. Basic winter supplies for a family of six can cost more than $6,000 inside Gaza, compared with about $700 when aid agencies buy them abroad and bring them in, the NRC said. Donors have funded only 35 percent of the $283m needed for the minimum winter shelter response.

A tent crossing the border tells a family little about when help will reach its camp. In al-Mawasi, near Khan Younis, Fadi Wafi told the Palestinian news agency Wafa on Wednesday that his name had been put on a list of people affected by the last storm, but he had received no shelter supplies. His family of five had two mattresses and two blankets.

What can be done before the next storm?

Gaza’s Government Media Office warned on Tuesday that it expected another storm within days. Aid workers have cleared drains, reinforced shelters and put up flood barriers, but OCHA reported on November 20 that such work had been recorded at only 162 of the 356 flood-prone locations that teams were tracking.

On Monday, IOM said Israeli authorities had approved about 70,000 pieces of timber and more than 1,200 toolkits to build sturdier emergency shelters for about 1,200 families. COGAT also said it had approved pumps and generators and would allow partial repairs at the Sheikh Ijlin and Sheikh Radwan sewage facilities. It did not say the equipment had arrived. COGAT has said reconstruction equipment will enter only after Hamas has fully disarmed. Gaza’s municipalities are still asking for pumps, backup generators and fuel.

For Om Hani Hamouda, whose family has been displaced about 15 times, the question is what they can live in when it rains again. “We want these tents to be replaced with caravans,” she told Al Jazeera after her tent flooded in az-Zawayda. “Even a simple caravan would be better.”

articles.body:
The number of young people across the UK not in education, employment or training (Neet) has decreased but remains close to a million as Andy Burnham’s government pushes to tackle Britain’s youth jobs crisis.

As ministers prepare to make sweeping changes in response to Alan Milburn’s landmark report on young people and work, the Office for National Statistics said the number of Neets fell by 22,000 in the three months to September, to 959,000.

On an annual basis, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds not earning or learning was 17,000 higher than a year ago. Although down from a peak of just over a million in March, the latest figure remains close to the highest level in a decade.

The prime minister last week promised to create an entirely new welfare system for young people after Milburn said Britain risked “losing a generation of young people” without a radical change in course.

Milburn also called for a radical shake-up of employment support to guarantee young people would get help, alongside changes to education policy and healthcare.

A parallel review into disability benefits by the Labour minister Stephen Timms this week called for significant changes to a welfare system that was “no longer fit for purpose”.

Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said young people deserved better. “That’s why we’re fundamentally reforming how we support young people to grow up in this country,” he said. “As part of our response to the Milburn review, we’re building a new settlement that invests in young people’s success instead of paying for failure.”

It is understood the government is preparing a full response to Milburn’s recommendations spelling out the changes that will be made. Ministers will then publish a white paper next year on welfare reform.

Overhauling welfare will, however, stand as one of the biggest challenges for Burnham’s government as he pushes to curb a rising welfare bill without triggering a repeat of the backbench rebellion faced by Keir Starmer.

Business leaders last week seized on elements of Milburn’s report calling for tax cuts and for the government to take a more cautious approach on its plan to boost workers’ rights, which he said could hit youth hiring. Bosses have blamed Labour for adding to employment costs, increasing the pressure on companies amid surging inflation triggered by the war in the Middle East.

Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, said: “Since Labour took power they have killed jobs for young people, with their jobs tax and Employment Rights Act. Labour’s solution of throwing taxpayers’ money at subsidised work placements will do nothing to fix the underlying problems.”

According to the latest snapshot from the ONS, one in eight young people in the UK were Neet in the three months to September – down slightly from the level in June but largely unchanged from a year earlier.

The drop in the three months to September was driven by a decline in the number of 18- to 24-year-old Neets to 867,000. However, the number of 16- and 17-year-olds finishing their education without finding work or training rose to 92,000 – the highest level since 2012.

Iona Ledwidge, the chief executive of the youth employment charity Spear, said: “While any decrease in these figures is welcome, they remain far too high. Rolling out the support that Alan Milburn recommended can’t come soon enough. Even six months out of work damages a young person’s wellbeing.”

articles.title: EU leaders struggle to agree on long-term budget, $49bn Ukraine loan
articles.summary: The bloc is holding an extraordinary summit in Brussels to discuss its budget proposal for 2028 to 2034.
articles.preview: The bloc is holding an extraordinary summit in Brussels to discuss its budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 as well as a new loan for Ukraine. European Union leaders are struggling to reach a deal on the bloc’s nearly $1.76 trillion budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 and agree a new $49bn loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year.
articles.body:
The bloc is holding an extraordinary summit in Brussels to discuss its budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 as well as a new loan for Ukraine.

European Union leaders are struggling to reach a deal on the bloc’s nearly $1.76 trillion budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 and agree a new $49bn loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year.

The differences were visible at an extraordinary EU summit in Brussels on Thursday, where some leaders called for belts to be tightened, while others defended traditional policies that consume large parts of the budget.

Most, however, wanted extra funds for important new priorities and to help Ukraine almost five years into the war.

“Europe needs solid finances. We can’t and we mustn’t take on more debt,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, in remarks that highlighted some of the contradictions. “At the same time, there is a series of tasks we must fulfil reliably.”

“The priorities must be a flourishing economy, the internal market must be able to develop its full potential, and we need better defence,” he told reporters.

Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Hungary’s Prime Minister Peter Magyar were more forthright.

“We’re light-years away from a solution,” Meloni told reporters before the summit. “We are not willing to sign off on a budget under which we would have to give more to receive less,” she added.

“Hearing the completely opposing positions in the room, the chance of an agreement today is virtually zero, but a Christmas agreement does not seem likely either,” Magyar posted on Facebook.

Unanimous approval

The new joint spending package is small compared with national budgets and is financed mostly by the 27 member countries based on the size of their economies. But it does require unanimous approval from all member states.

While the budget only starts in 2028, leaders want to have a deal by year-end because there are elections next year in France, Italy, Poland, Greece, Estonia, Finland and Slovakia that could complicate negotiations.

“The budget needs to be modernised and needs to be downsized if we want to strike a deal,” Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said as he arrived for the summit. “I’m ready for this marathon, if it ends today, tomorrow or somewhere in December.”

European Council President Antonio Costa, who is chairing the summit that could run into Friday, called on the leaders to approach the debate with an “open mind, a constructive approach and the sense of compromise”.

He said that an agreement is needed “by the end of this year and for this we need to reach unanimity”.

The Ukraine puzzle

Ukraine is a big part of the EU’s budget puzzle. The spending package foresees $110bn for the government in Kyiv over seven years. The leaders must also decide on the new loan and whether the costs of servicing it should be drawn from the budget.

Earlier this month, Merz threatened to hold up a budget agreement if no “collective commitment” was made to Ukraine by all member countries, “without exception”.

Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia oppose using funds for military aid to Ukraine. Merz repeated his warning on Thursday and said that “we will talk about this in depth in one-on-one talks”.

“We must ensure that Ukraine receives sufficient support in the coming years,” Merz said as he entered the summit. “I don’t think anyone in Europe can have any interest in seeing new waves of refugees from Ukraine if this war does not come to an end.”

Nearly a year ago, EU leaders endorsed a loan of $99bn to cover most of the Ukrainian government’s needs for two years. But Russia’s intensified attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure, along with disruptions to Black Sea trade, are straining Ukraine’s finances.

articles.title: US-backed Ebola quarantine centre violated constitution, Kenyan court rules
articles.summary: A Kenyan court on Thursday ruled that the government had breached the constitution by allowing the construction of a US-backed Ebola quarantine site at a military base in Laikipia.
articles.preview: Kenya Kenya’s government violated the Constitution by allowing the construction of a US-backed Ebola quarantine facility without public participation, a senior court ruled on Thursday. The 50-bed facility at a military base in Laikipia sparked deadly protests by residents who feared exposure to the virus and an outbreak that could overwhelm Kenya's fragile health system.
articles.body:
Kenya

Kenya’s government violated the Constitution by allowing the construction of a US-backed Ebola quarantine facility without public participation, a senior court ruled on Thursday.

The 50-bed facility at a military base in Laikipia sparked deadly protests by residents who feared exposure to the virus and an outbreak that could overwhelm Kenya's fragile health system.

In May, the High Court had ordered construction of the facility to be halted pending the determination of a case filed by the Law Society of Kenya and constitutional watchdog Katiba Institute. The petitioners argued that Kenya’s fragile health system was ill-equipped to handle a potential Ebola outbreak.

Trump administration officials had said Americans exposed to Ebola abroad would be sent to the facility rather than flown home. The US government planned to commit $13.5 million to Kenya’s Ebola preparedness efforts.

Justice Patricia Nyaundi on Thursday ordered the government to disclose all agreements with the US within 45 days. She also barred further construction or operations at the facility.

Residents reported seeing military aircraft landing at the base shortly after construction began. A US-based humanitarian group also said some of its staff members who had been working in Congo had been quarantined in Kenya.

Kenya reported its first-ever Ebola case in October, after a Kenyan national traveled from Congo through Uganda. The country recorded a total of nine cases, all involving direct contacts of the initial patient.

Asked in October whether the US-backed facility would also quarantine Kenyans exposed to Ebola, Health Minister Aden Duale said the government was awaiting the court’s directions.

articles.title: Iraq closes two border crossings in Kurdistan region with Syria and Iran
articles.summary: Iraq closes two border crossings in Kurdistan region with Syria and Iran Iraqi border forces have closed two border crossings with Syria and Iran that had been administered by the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG), state media reported, as Baghdad moves to assert more control over the semi-autonomous region. The al-Waleed crossing with Syria and the Bashta crossing with Iran, both located in territory administered by the Kurdistan region, have been closed, the commander of Iraq's border forces told the Iraqi News Agency. The closures follow a ruling by Iraq's highest court on Wednesday allowing Baghdad to deploy federal forces along all international borders, including in the Kurdistan region.

articles.title: Protests in Iraqi Kurdistan at plans for government in Baghdad to take over oil, border crossings
articles.summary: Thousands have gathered in the capital of northern Iraq's semiautonomous Kurdish region, waving flags and voicing opposition to plans for the federal government to take control of oil operations and border crossings.
articles.preview: Mass protests in Kurdish Irbil against Iraqi government reform plans November 26, 2026 Thousands have gathered in the capital of northern Iraq's semiautonomous Kurdish region, waving flags and voicing opposition to plans for the federal government to take control of oil operations and border crossings. Protesters took to the streets of Irbil, also often written Erbil, in Iraqi Kurdistan early on Thursday in large numbers, waving massive flags of the semiautonomous region in northern Iraq.
articles.body:
Mass protests in Kurdish Irbil against Iraqi government reform plans

November 26, 2026

Thousands have gathered in the capital of northern Iraq's semiautonomous Kurdish region, waving flags and voicing opposition to plans for the federal government to take control of oil operations and border crossings.

Protesters took to the streets of Irbil, also often written Erbil, in Iraqi Kurdistan early on Thursday in large numbers, waving massive flags of the semiautonomous region in northern Iraq.

They were responding to federal government plans announced earlier in the week for Baghdad to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had said the measures were part of a bid to stop oil smuggling when announcing the changes.

Rival Kurdish factions unite to protest plans

The plans marked an escalation in the long-running power struggle between the central government and Kurdish authorities that have largely governed themselves since 1991, albeit with varying levels of recognition and authority.

Rival Kurdish parties joined forces for the large protests in the regional capital.

Protests were also reported to have spread to several other towns and cities beyond the capital.

Iraq's 2005 constitution, written following the US-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein, formally recognized the Kurdish region and its government. But authorities in Erbil and Baghdad have remained in a tug of war over the control of land, oil and money ever since.

Tuesday's decision, which received backing from Iraq's Federal Supreme Court a day later, brings border crossing in the Kurdish region under federal government management. It places approval for oil exports from the region under the authority of the federal oil ministry and transfers the management of oil fields in four contested provinces — Kirkuk, Diyala, Salahuddin and Nineveh.

The Kurdish regional government's Cabinet said on Wednesday that the decision from Baghdad "violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan region," saying it represented "an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime."

Prime Minister al-Zaidi, who took office earlier this year with the backing of US President Donald Trump, also dismissed Kirkuk's operations commander and police chief and the head of the Border Ports Commission. He said the measures reflected Iraq's "independent national will."

Regional Prime Minister Masrour Barzani said his government was "surprised" by al-Zaidi's decisions and called them "completely unacceptable."

Contested region even since 2005 reformation

Iraq's Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that the authority of the Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) only covered the land it administered on March 19, 2003, the day before the US-led invasion that unseated Saddam Hussein.

Kurdish peshmerga forces moved into many disputed areas after 2003, including the oil fields covered by this week's orders.

The 2005 constitution tried to solve the fate of some of the disputed territories in the lands between the borders to Syria and Iran that are home to a host of ethnicities and communities but with Kurds generally the majority group.

Article 140 called for reversing Saddam-era policies of expelling Kurds and moving Arabs in, and called for a census and a referendum on whether the disputed regions should join the Kurdistan region. Neither was held.

Kurdish forces then gained more of the disputed territory after Iraqi forces were forced out by the so-called "Islamic State," with Kurdish pershmerga for subsequently reclaiming some of the land with some international assistance.

The oil-rich region is highly important to both administrations, in a country that relies on oil revenues for the vast majority of its public sector budget.

Internal political tensions within Iraqi Kurdistan have further complicated the issue in recent months, with the Federal Supreme Court hearing an ongoing challenge against the current government's legitimacy after a party withdrew from the coalition cabinet. But rival Kurdish political factions seem to have found common ground on this issue at least.

Il decimo film del regista iraniano, ispirato a Breve storia d’amore di Krzysztof Kieślowski è un film interamente francese per il cast, la lingua e le ambientazioni. Sylvie (Huppert), scrittrice misantropa, per comporre la sua opera s’ispira a quello che accade nell’appartamento di fronte al suo. Con un certo virtuosismo Farhadi orchestra un complesso gioco di apparenze, perdendosi però per strada. In questo ritratto d’artista impostore finiamo per intravedere quello di un regista spinto, anche per ciò che accade nel suo paese, dall’urgenza di ridefinirsi.

Jacques Mandelbaum, Le Monde

Stati Uniti 2026, 195’. In sala

Le nuove disavventure di Cliff Booth unisce la regia meticolosa di David Fincher e la narrazione irriverente di Quentin Tarantino, dando vita a un sequel accattivante e sgangherato di C’era una volta a… Hollywood. I punti di forza di Fincher e di Tarantino sono evidenti in una pellicola la cui riuscita è dovuta soprattutto a Brad Pitt, che riprende con fascino e pathos il ruolo che lo portò all’Oscar. Nell’estate del 1977, Cliff si arrangia come può in una Los Angeles che sta diventando irriconoscibile. Tutto cambia quando incontra Karen (Debicki), agente di una star televisiva megalomane.

Tim Grierson, Screen International

Stati Uniti / Germania 2026, 104’. In sala

Un gruppo di medici volontari in alcuni villaggi lungo il rio delle Amazzoni viene a conoscenza della leggenda di Boiúna poco prima che una violenta faida tra loschi personaggi risvegli il gigantesco serpente della giungla. Nonostante il contesto e alcune evidenti attinenze, questo survival horror non è un reboot di Anaconda ed è sicuramente superiore agli altri tentativi di sfruttarne il successo.

Megan Navarro, BloodyDisgusting

Alla vigilia della primavera di Praga, il giovane Tomáš ottiene un lavoro alla radio nazionale cecoslovacca, dove i giornalisti sfidano la censura di stato. Si ritrova nel cuore di un magnifico momento di resistenza giornalistica. Questo dramma politico non è rivoluzionario nella sua forma, cioè quella di una buona e solida ricostruzione, ma intreccia eventi personali e storici con una tale tensione che si comincia a sperare in un finale diverso da quello di una primavera repressa con la forza.

Guillemette Odicino, Télérama

Gemma Blasco affronta il tema dei traumi delle donne sopravvissute alla violenza con notevole sensibilità e moderazione. Sceglie di esplorare le conseguenze dello stupro subìto dalla protagonista attraverso una narrazione non lineare che riflette il suo disorientamento, la sua solitudine e il suo tormento emotivo. Ne risulta un film profondamente introspettivo che non solo mette a nudo il carico personale del trauma, ma s’interroga anche su come gli altri reagiscono a esso, in particolare su come il dolore della vittima possa essere sfruttato da coloro che le offrono aiuto.

articles.title: Africa's opposition voices face growing pressure
articles.summary: Opposition politicians and government critics say arrests, prosecutions and restrictions on public activity are making it harder to challenge those in power. Is a broader pattern emerging?
articles.preview: November 26, 2026 Opposition politicians and government critics say arrests, prosecutions and restrictions on public activity are making it harder to challenge those in power. Is a broader pattern emerging? articles.body:
November 26, 2026

Opposition politicians and government critics say arrests, prosecutions and restrictions on public activity are making it harder to challenge those in power. Is a broader pattern emerging?

From Cameroon and Tanzania to Mozambique, Nigeria and Zambia, opposition leaders have accused authorities of limiting political freedoms through legal action and restrictions on public activity.

In each case, officials have said the measures are justified under national laws and security provisions.

"Cameroon is very sensitive, and it is important that we know when to criticize the government and when not to criticize the government openly," said Ngam Glory Ani Mbom, a citizen of the central African country.

She said fear of arrest and violence discourage political participation. "You cannot talk about democracy when opposition supporters cannot freely express their minds to the public," she told DW.

For Ndah Grimbald, deputy secretary-general of Cameroon's opposition Social Democratic Front, one of the biggest obstacles is organizing public meetings.

"The first major challenge we face as members of the opposition is the non-authorization of public rallies, public meetings," he said, noting that opposition proposals receive little attention in parliament. "Private members' bills are not even listened to."

Cameroonian law guarantees freedom of assembly but allows authorities to restrict gatherings on grounds of public order or national security. Organizers are also required to notify officials in advance.

Tanzania: Trial and prison

In Tanzania, opposition leader Tundu Lissu was arrested in April 2025 and charged with treason. In November 2026, the High Court acquitted Lissu of treason but convicted him of incitement and sentenced him to four years in prison.

Prosecutors argued that Lissu's remarks were intended to disrupt Tanzania's 2025 general election. In its ruling, the court said it was satisfied that his statements were intended to "disrupt elections and instigate violence."

Lissu rejected the verdict, calling the case "political persecution." He told the judges: "I was not charged with incitement but you judges are convicting me with it just to impress the person who gives you the titles." He added: "Excuses were created to imprison me."

Gerson Msigwa, Tanzania's chief government spokesperson, directly rejected allegations of political repression and human rights violations.

"Concerns of diminishing civic space and restrictions on political parties to engage in political processes in the lead-up to the general election are unfounded and misleading," Msigwa said in response to Amnesty International's accusations of a "wave of terror" sweeping Tanzania ahead of the 2025 vote.

Mozambique: Charges disputed

In Mozambique, opposition figure Venancio Mondlane faces five charges linked to protests after the disputed 2024 election, including incitement to terrorism and public advocacy of crime. Prosecutors have accused him of encouraging violence and civil disobedience. Mondlane has denied the allegations.

"I have more than enough evidence. There's plenty to go around. Many of my statements were precisely in the opposite direction," he told DW, adding that the protests were intended to prevent violence.

Pedro Sinai Nhatitima, a judge counselor and spokesperson for Mozambique's Supreme Court, defended the court's decision not to allow live broadcasts of Mondlane's trial. He denied that the proceedings are politically influenced, saying the court will decide the case according to the law.

Nigeria: Policing dissent?

In Nigeria, police in Borno State recently arrested five men wearing T-shirts bearing the slogan "Tinubu Must Go!"

The police said the men were not arrested for their political views, but were found with suspected drugs and other items. The men face allegations including public disturbance and thuggery.

In Kano, police blocked access to a venue for a planned meeting, citing public safety concerns.

Zambia: Courts and controversy

In Zambia, opposition leader Brian Mundubile has criticized what he describes as a retreat from democratic rights. The courts were closed on August 24, the final day for filing a presidential election petition. The judiciary cited security reasons, while police said intelligence-led security assessments were underway at several government institutions.

State House presidential aide Clayson Hamasaka denied that President Hakainde Hichilema had ordered the closure to prevent an election challenge.

The same month, former opposition lawmaker and cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot dead during a security operation at Mundubile's residence. Authorities said the operation followed intelligence about individuals considered a national security threat, and that officers came under gunfire and returned fire.

Mundubile, who faces treason and sedition charges with other opposition figures, has called for fairness in the proceedings. "We expect an open court process. We are innocent of all the charges against us," he said.

Zambian constitutional lawyer Linda Kasonde has warned: "As you can see, our public institutions are on trial. Democracy in Zambia is on trial."

Cameroonian political analyst Kinang Derick Fai said that despite the setbacks, democratic development across the continent remains a work in progress.

"We are far from getting to the best level," he said. "It is a democracy still struggling to find its way."

DW correspondent Moki Edwin Kindzeka contributed reporting.

articles.title: Senegal parliament denounces president over budget decree
articles.summary: Senegal's parliament on Wednesday adopted a resolution criticizing President Bassirou Diomaye Faye's decision ​to implement a budget bill for 2026 that ‌lawmakers had previously rejected
articles.preview: Senegal Senegal's parliament on Wednesday adopted a resolution criticizing President Bassirou Diomaye Faye's decision to implement a budget bill for 2026 that lawmakers had previously rejected. Last week, the President ordered into force by decree a budget bill seen as crucial to restoring public finances as the country finalises an International Monetary Fund (IMF) bailout.
articles.body:
Senegal

Senegal's parliament on Wednesday adopted a resolution criticizing President Bassirou Diomaye Faye's decision to implement a budget bill for 2026 that lawmakers had previously rejected.

Last week, the President ordered into force by decree a budget bill seen as crucial to restoring public finances as the country finalises an International Monetary Fund (IMF) bailout.

Senegal is embroiled in a political and budgetary impasse, with Faye at loggerheads with the National Assembly, where the opposition Pastef party holds an enormous majority and is hostile to his budget measures.

Pastef leader Ousmane Sonko, an archrival of the president, is known for his disdain for debt restructuring which is required under the IMF loan.

Lawmakers voted 128 to 9 in favour of Wednesday's resolution.

In September, Senegal announced it had struck a $2.2 billion IMF debt programme aimed at stabilising its public finances.

But the IMF has yet to announce executive board approval and the bailout is subject to certain conditions.

articles.title: In cammino con Patti Smith e i Soundwalk Collective
articles.summary: La cantante statunitense ha presentato in anteprima la sua mostra a Milano insieme al musicista Stephan Crasneanscki
articles.preview: Patti Smith cammina nelle sale della Triennale di Milano, dove sta presentando in anteprima la mostra Correspondences. I giornalisti la seguono come uno sciame, puntandole addosso telefoni, macchine fotografiche e telecamere. articles.body:
Patti Smith cammina nelle sale della Triennale di Milano, dove sta presentando in anteprima la mostra Correspondences. I giornalisti la seguono come uno sciame, puntandole addosso telefoni, macchine fotografiche e telecamere. Lei non si scompone, e tiene in mano una matita, con cui ogni tanto scrive delle parole su alcuni disegni appesi al muro.

“Questa la finirò più tardi”, commenta riferendosi a un’opera che, ci racconta, è ispirata a Leonardo da Vinci e al brano Power of soul di Jimi Hendrix.

L’esposizione, curata dalla poeta e cantante statunitense insieme ai due musicisti del progetto Soundwalk Collective, il francese Stephan Crasneanscki e l’italiano Simone Merli, e realizzata in collaborazione con la Fondation Cartier, sarà in programma dal 26 novembre al 7 marzo e intreccia musica, film e poesia. Il 26 e il 27 novembre, inoltre, Smith e i Soundwalk Collective la trasformano in una performance dal vivo al Teatro lirico Giorgio Gaber, per il festival Terraforma.

Smith collabora con i Soundwalk Collective da più di dieci anni. Un giorno durante un viaggio in aereo ha conosciuto per caso Stephan Crasneanscki, sound artist francese trapiantato negli Stati Uniti, scoprendo di avere molte cose in comune con lui.

Da quel momento i due hanno cominciato a scambiarsi registrazioni, testi, idee e suggestioni. Una corrispondenza artistica che li ha portati a pubblicare diversi singoli ed ep a cavallo tra elettronica, sperimentazione e spoken word.

Crasneanscki è specializzato nei field recordings (registrazioni sul campo), che realizza anche in aree remote del mondo, e nella creazioni di tappeti sonori su cui Smith registra le sue parti vocali, attingendo alle poesie che ha scritto in passato e a testi scritti per l’occasione. Proprio da quei brani è nata la mostra, che ha debuttato in Europa ad Arles a luglio e ora è arrivata a Milano.

Alla Triennale Patti Smith, che il 30 dicembre compirà ottant’anni, continua a parlare delle opere. Lo farà senza sosta per quasi due ore, fermandosi solo un paio di minuti per mangiare una caramella e bere un bicchier d’acqua per calmare la tosse. Negli enormi schermi che pendono dal soffitto scene dei film Medea di Pasolini e Andrej Rublëv di Tarkovskij si alternano a video di oceani e foreste in fiamme.

Tra i temi centrali di Correspondences, del resto, c’è il cambiamento climatico, presente anche nel nuovo brano dei Soundwalk Collective Cry of the lost, dedicato all’inquinamento acustico negli oceani. Ma non è l’unico argomento della mostra.

Su una parete la cantante mostra una foto scattata da una fotografa palestinese uccisa dai bombardamenti israeliani, su cui Smith ha scritto i nomi di alcuni dei bambini morti a Gaza. Dagli altoparlanti a un certo punto viene diffuso un coro di bambine russe, estratto dal brano dei Soundwalk Collective Children of Chernobyl, dedicato alle vittime del disastro nucleare del 1986.

L’arte non basta

“Noi artisti non possiamo offrire soluzioni ai problemi che affliggono l’umanità, ma possiamo rendere le persone più consapevoli”, racconta Patti Smith dopo la fine della presentazione e gli immancabili selfie a cui si è prestata per almeno quindici minuti.

Lei e Stephan Crasneanscki sono seduti su un tavolo di legno dentro a Casa Lana, una sala della Triennale ispirata a un progetto dall’architetto Ettore Sottsass. Per terra c’è la moquette rossa, intorno librerie arredate con oggetti vintage e poltrone colorate. La cantante si toglie gli occhiali, si sistema i lunghi capelli bianchi e la giacca scura che porta sopra a un paio di jeans. Crasneanscki, alto ed elegante, indossa un completo scuro.

“In alcune zone del mondo le persone sono più attente a temi come la crisi climatica, ma nel mio paese, gli Stati Uniti, non è sempre così”, dice Patti Smith. “Al governo di Donald Trump non interessa l’ambiente, e così mente alle persone. Ho visto visitatori sconvolti dai video che proiettiamo durante la mostra sulle foreste che bruciano in Siberia, in Canada e in California. L’arte da sola non può cambiare le cose, ma le persone possono farlo, per questo è a loro che ci rivolgiamo”.

Mentre Smith parla, mi viene in mente A hard rain’s a-gonna fall di Bob Dylan, una metafora sulle catastrofi globali d’ispirazione biblica scritta negli anni sessanta che, ad ascoltarlo oggi, sembra aver quasi predetto i cambiamenti climatici. Un pezzo che nel 2016 la stessa Smith ha cantato dal vivo, commuovendosi, alla cerimonia di consegna del premio Nobel, dove si è presentata per ritirare il premio al posto di Dylan.

“Quando ho sentito la canzone per la prima volta, nel 1963”, racconta, “ero una ragazzina e vivevo in una zona rurale. Mi colpì la sua poesia, il suo linguaggio alla Rimbaud, mal al tempo stesso mi aprì anche gli occhi su quello che stava succedendo nel mondo, sull’inquinamento e la distruzione del nostro ambiente. Mi è successa la stessa cosa con Neil Young, con Joan Baez e con Jimi Hendrix, tutti artisti che amo, persone di pace”.

Che effetto fa ai due musicisti vedere le persone camminare in mezzo alle loro opere? “Nella mostra”, spiega Stephan Crasneanscki, “cerchiamo di aprire una conversazione con il pubblico, è diverso da un concerto. Anche la concezione del tempo cambia quando abiti questo spazio, diventa ciclica. È come non ci fossero più un presente, un passato e un futuro”.

E danno fastidio tutti quei telefoni puntati addosso? “Vent’anni fa non avevo nemmeno il cellulare”, risponde Patti Smith. “A un certo punto l’ho dovuto comprare, perché non c’erano più cabine telefoniche a New York. All’inizio quando mi fermavano per fare le foto o puntavano i telefoni verso di me ai concerti mi arrabbiavo e pensavo: ‘Sto cercando di comunicare con voi, mettete via quei cazzo di telefoni!’”.

“Oggi, che ho quasi ottant’anni”, continua, “penso che il mio lavoro non sia fare la poliziotta con le nuove generazioni o con chiunque usi un telefono, ci penseranno da soli a gestire la dipendenza dagli schermi”. Alcuni musicisti, però, ne vietano l’uso durante le loro esibizioni. “Qualche giorno fa sono stata a un concerto di Bob, e lui è contro questa cosa. Ha 85 anni, ci ha dato tantissimo ed è giusto che decida in quali condizioni si vuole esibire. Quel giorno ho deciso di lasciare direttamente il telefono a casa”.

Elevazione spirituale

Nella mostra Correspondences la figura di Pierpaolo Pasolini torna spesso. Oltre a Medea, sugli schermi vengono proiettate delle scene del film di Abel Ferrara dedicato al regista e scrittore friulano. Smith e i Soundwalk Collective hanno anche scritto un brano intitolato Pasolini, che ruota proprio attorno alla morte dell’intellettuale, avvenuta a Ostia nel 1975.

“Sono stata cresciuta seguendo la fede cristiana”, spiega Patti Smith, “e nella mia famiglia l’arte non era considerata una cosa necessaria per l’elevazione spirituale. Io però volevo essere un’artista, e soprattutto volevo essere libera, quindi ho rinnegato la religione. Poi ho visto Il vangelo secondo Matteo di Pasolini e per me è cambiato tutto: Gesù in quel film è un rivoluzionario che insegna che dio è ovunque, e quindi è accessibile a tutti”.

“Leone XIV”,continua, “parla ogni volta dell’importanza degli artisti per il genere umano. Il nostro lavoro con il progetto Soundwalk Collective è spirituale in modo innato, ma non ha nessun dogma al suo interno. Semplicemente crediamo che, come diceva quella frase attribuita a Leonardo Da Vinci, ‘la conoscenza di tutte le cose è possibile’”.

Nei prossimi mesi usciranno altri singoli del progetto Soundwalk Collective, a partire da Correspondences vol III, in arrivo a gennaio, in cui è contenuta proprio Cry of the lost. “Non facciamo canzoni per la radio, ovviamente”, spiega Crasneanscki, “ma ci piace questa cosa di pubblicare vinili con solo due brani, con un lato a e un lato b. Non mettere troppe informazioni in questi pezzi, perché sono molto densi. Io li definisco più che altro dei paesaggi sonori”

“Quando compongo cose insieme a Stephan”, aggiunge Patti Smith prima di salutarmi,“parto sempre da un dialogo interiore, da quello che ascolto nella mia mente. E mi piace abitare questi paesaggi sonori, mi piace che chi ascolta li viva in prima persona. Del resto ci chiamiamo Soundwalk Collective, vogliamo che le persone camminino al nostro fianco”. ◆

articles.title: Ucraina, Kushner: 'Putin ha mostrato finora moderazione non usando armi nucleari'
articles.summary: Kiev: 'Non abbiamo alcuna intenzione di estendere la guerra alla Libia'
articles.preview: L'Ucraina non stava cercando di estendere la guerra con la Russia alle coste libiche attaccando due navi russe al largo di Bengasi: lo ha dichiarato il ministro degli Esteri ucraino, Andrij Sybiha. In un post su X, Sybiha ha riferito di aver contattato il suo omologo libico, Al-Taher Al-Baour, per chiarire che "nessuna azione dell'Ucraina è mai stata diretta contro la Libia o il popolo libico, ma esclusivamente contro obiettivi militari russi che servono direttamente la guerra della Russia".
articles.body:
L'Ucraina non stava cercando di estendere la guerra con la Russia alle coste libiche attaccando due navi russe al largo di Bengasi: lo ha dichiarato il ministro degli Esteri ucraino, Andrij Sybiha. In un post su X, Sybiha ha riferito di aver contattato il suo omologo libico, Al-Taher Al-Baour, per chiarire che "nessuna azione dell'Ucraina è mai stata diretta contro la Libia o il popolo libico, ma esclusivamente contro obiettivi militari russi che servono direttamente la guerra della Russia". "Non abbiamo alcuna intenzione di estendere la guerra della Russia contro l'Ucraina alla Libia o a qualsiasi altro Paese", ha aggiunto.

Il presidente russo Vladimir Putin ha "dimostrato moderazione" non utilizzando armi nucleari nel conflitto con l'Ucraina, ha affermato l'inviato della Casa Bianca Jared Kushner, definendo il leader russo un "grande uomo di politica". In un'ampia intervista per il podcast 'MD Meets', ripreso da Bbc, il genero di Donald Trump ha affermato di essere convinto che Putin desideri la pace. "Finora Putin ha mostrato moderazione; ha accettato di non usare armi nucleari, il che ovviamente è un fatto di grande importanza, e ci ha rassicurato che non è questa la sua intenzione. È senza dubbio un grande uomo della politica, una figura storica".

La presidente della Commissione europea, Ursula von der Leyen, difficilmente può aspirare a un ruolo di mediatore nella risoluzione del conflitto ucraino avanzando ultimatum alla Russia. Lo ha affermato il portavoce del Cremlino, Dmitry Peskov, dopo che ieri von der Leyen aveva detto che la Ue parteciperà al prossimo round di negoziati e che la Russia deve sospendere gli attacchi alle infrastrutture energetiche. "La Russia non deve nulla, la Russia deve garantire i propri interessi nazionali", ha affermato Peskov in un'intervista alla televisione di Stato ripresa dall'agenzia Interfax.

"Penso che la guerra non si debba e non si possa allargare al Mediterraneo. Penso che su questo dobbiamo essere molto chiari con i nostri amici ucraini e dobbiamo essere chiari anche con i nostri partner. Penso che dobbiamo anche fare del nostro meglio per continuare ad aiutare l'Ucraina a difendersi". Lo afferma la presidente del Consiglio Giorgia Meloni a margine del Consiglio europeo a Bruxelles.

Filorussi, 'almeno 5 morti per attacco droni ucraini in regione Zaporizhzhia'

Cinque persone sono state uccise in un attacco con droni ucraini nella regione ucraina di Zaporizhzhia sotto il controllo delle forze di Mosca. articles.title: Attack on Saudi’s Jazan refinery kills one person, disrupts operations
articles.summary: The attack killed a Nepali national, injured several people and sparked a fire, Saudi Energy Ministry says.
articles.preview: The attack killed a Nepali national, injured several people and sparked a fire, Saudi Energy Ministry says. An aerial projectile has hit an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia’s city of Jazan, killing one worker and injuring several other people, according to the country’s Ministry of Energy. Thursday’s attack on the facility on the kingdom’s Red Sea coast caused a fire and temporarily halted some operations, the ministry said.
articles.body:
The attack killed a Nepali national, injured several people and sparked a fire, Saudi Energy Ministry says.

An aerial projectile has hit an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia’s city of Jazan, killing one worker and injuring several other people, according to the country’s Ministry of Energy.

Thursday’s attack on the facility on the kingdom’s Red Sea coast caused a fire and temporarily halted some operations, the ministry said.

The statement did not identify who carried out the strike, but earlier the Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said that the Iranian-backed group had attacked the refinery. It came after Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency had issued an alert about potential danger in Jazan province.

The strike was the Houthis‘ latest blow against key Saudi facilities, a day after the group claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, the kingdom’s largest refinery and a major crude export hub, and the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, amid escalating hostilities between the two sides.

The Saudi Ministry of Energy said the worker who died was Nepali, while the injured were of various nationalities.

The injured received medical care, while emergency personnel and specialised technical teams arrived at the site to assess the damage and verify the safety of the facilities following the attack, the ministry added.

The refinery in southwestern Saudi Arabia, near the Yemeni border, is designed to process up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day.

The Saudi-led coalition, which is backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government in its fight with the Houthis, condemned the strike and threatened a counterattack.

“Targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure would be met with a firm military response,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki posted on X.

Later on Thursday, the coalition claimed its forces had destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launch platform in Yemen’s Hodeidah governorate used by the armed group to stage the attack on the Jazan refinery, according to al-Maliki. There was no immediate statement from the Houthis regarding the strike.

Fighting in Yemen

On the ground in Yemen, meanwhile, Saudi-backed government forces claimed they had carried out 767 strikes on Houthi positions on Thursday.

In a post on X, the forces’ spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili said the strikes had “neutralised” 117 Houthi fighters and destroyed 87 vehicles and combat assets.

Al-Nuzaili added that government forces continued to confront Houthi formations on the front lines in northern and western Marib governorate, as well as in the governorates of al-Jawf, Taiz, Lahj, Shabwah and Hajjah.

Earlier on Thursday, a series of air strikes targeted Yemen’s Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, according to media affiliated with the armed group, which is also known as Ansar Allah – Arabic for Supporters of God.

Elsewhere, Houthi forces targeted Habib al-Sarm and al-Hujalla, as well as al-Aqroud in al-Masrakh district.

The Houthis, who control the most populous areas of Yemen, have launched missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and office buildings since the country’s civil war reignited in July, in a spillover from the US-Iran war.

The attacks have previously temporarily disrupted some of Aramco’s operations and caused the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh. They also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including football’s AFC Asian Cup and the flagship FII investment conference.

The fighting has also exacerbated dire humanitarian conditions for Yemeni civilians.

The World Health Organization (WHO) reported that as of Monday, 2,361 people had been killed and 10,982 injured since fighting in Yemen escalated in August. More than 360,000 people have also been forced to flee their homes in Yemen since the start of August, according to the UN.

articles.title: Attacco con droni in Kuwait, morti due tecnici italiani
articles.summary: "E' stato l'Iran". Ma Teheran sente Tajani e nega, 'pronti ad inchiesta congiunta'
articles.preview: Erano impegnati a fare manutenzione ai radar del sistema di difesa antiaerea Skyguard in dotazione alle forze armate kuwaitiane. Due tecnici italiani sono rimasti uccisi in Kuwait in seguito ad un attacco di droni: Antonio Saccoccio, 65 anni, di Formia ed Emanuele Lo Russo, 36 anni, di Roma. Lavoravano per Rheinmetall Italia. E' un'azione iraniana, indicano le autorità locali. Ed il ministro degli Esteri Antonio Tajani inizialmente annuncia: "ci lamenteremo con l'ambasciata dell'Iran per quello che è successo".
articles.body:
Erano impegnati a fare manutenzione ai radar del sistema di difesa antiaerea Skyguard in dotazione alle forze armate kuwaitiane. Due tecnici italiani sono rimasti uccisi in Kuwait in seguito ad un attacco di droni: Antonio Saccoccio, 65 anni, di Formia ed Emanuele Lo Russo, 36 anni, di Roma. Lavoravano per Rheinmetall Italia.

E' un'azione iraniana, indicano le autorità locali. Ed il ministro degli Esteri Antonio Tajani inizialmente annuncia: "ci lamenteremo con l'ambasciata dell'Iran per quello che è successo". Ma Teheran respinge in modo "categorico e assoluto" responsabilità nell'attacco.

In serata Tajani sente i colleghi di Kuwait e Iran ed informa che gli iraniani sono pronti a partecipare ad una commissione d'inchiesta congiunta per accertare quanto accaduto. Il ministero della Difesa kuwaitiano la racconta così: le forze armate hanno rilevato la presenza di "droni ostili" nello spazio aereo nazionale; l'"aggressione iraniana", prosegue lo statement, ha preso di mira "un sito vitale", provocando la caduta di schegge che hanno colpito quattro persone. I due italiani sono morti, mentre un kuwaitiano ed un pachistano sono rimasti feriti.

Il Kuwait, come gli altri Paesi del Golfo che ospitano presenze militari americane, è diventato un obiettivo per l'Iran dopo la guerra scatenata dagli Usa del marzo scorso. L'allarme nel Paese si era alzato ulteriormente pochi giorni fa: lo scorso 17 novembre l'esercito kuwaitiano ha informato di aver contrastato attacchi di droni. E l'esercito iraniano aveva subito rivendicato l'azione, spiegando di aver attaccato la base aerea di Ali al-Salem, dove opera un'aliquota dell'Aeronautica americana e fino a pochi mesi fa - prima del conflitto con l'Iran - c'era anche il contingente italiano con poco più di 200 effettivi.

E' stato il ministro della Difesa, Guido Crosetto, a comunicare alle Camere la "scelta di trasferire dei militari dal Kuwait all'interno della operazione Inherent Resolve, mettendoli in sicurezza in parte in Arabia Saudita e in parte in altri Paesi". Proprio per contrastare la minaccia dei droni, il Kuwait ospita sofisticati sistemi controaerei. Tra questi lo Skyguard di Rheinmetall Italia, che si compone di mitragliere, missili e radar per intercettare e neutralizzare gli sciami 'low cost' prodotti dall'Iran. Si tratta di sistemi che hanno bisogno di continua manutenzione e per questo il Kuwait si avvaleva dei tecnici forniti direttamente dall'azienda sulla base di un contratto stipulato.

Profondo cordoglio per la morte dei due italiani è stato espresso dalla premier Giorgia Meloni, dai ministri e da politici di maggioranza ed opposizione. Solidarietà è arrivata anche dal ministro degli Esteri israeliano, Gideon Sa'ar: "l'aggressione incontrollata dell'Iran - afferma - minaccia la stabilità e la sicurezza in Medio Oriente e oltre. Deve finire". Ma il portavoce delle forze armate della Repubblica islamica nega: "nessuna operazione militare o offensiva è stata condotta dalle forze armate" iraniane nella regione e "considerando lo storico di azioni ostili, nonché il ruolo svolto dal regime sionista e dalle forze statunitensi nel ricorrere a tattiche 'false flag' e nell'intraprendere avventure nella regione, tali accuse vanno interpretate come un pretesto per celare una perdurante malevolenza e come un tentativo di esacerbare l'instabilità nell'area".

C'è stato quindi un contatto diretto tra Tajani ed il collega Abbas Araghchi, che ha espresso cordoglio per la morte degli italiani, ha definito infondate le accuse ed offerto la disponibilità a collaborare con il Kuwait per definire le responsabilità. Dagli accertamenti svolti, ha spiegato Tajani, "il drone è costruito in Iran e sappiamo che ci sono anche tante milizie proxy dell'Iran che utilizzano questi droni". Ci sono ad esempio gli Houthi, o anche fazioni filo-iraniane nel vicino Iraq. Comunque sia andata, è l'ennesima tragedia in un Medio Oriente in fiamme dove continuano a morire anche civili.

articles.title: La minaccia russa fa paura, Londra allerta 100.000 riservisti
articles.summary: 'Tenetevi pronti alla chiamata'. Non succedeva dai tempi della Guerra Fredda
articles.preview: Il tam tam dei tamburi di guerra torna a far sentire i suoi echi sinistri sulla vecchia Europa, sotto le insegne di una fraseologia bellica che sembrava consegnata agli incubi del passato. L'ultimo rintocco risuona nel Regno Unito, dove il ministro della Difesa, Wes Streeting, ha fatto inviare una lettera circolare a ben 100.000 riservisti, ex militari soggetti a richiamo in caso di emergenze, sollecitati a tenersi pronti a fronteggiare un orizzonte di "minacce rafforzate", fra conflitti e crisi geopolitiche internazionali.
articles.body:
Il tam tam dei tamburi di guerra torna a far sentire i suoi echi sinistri sulla vecchia Europa, sotto le insegne di una fraseologia bellica che sembrava consegnata agli incubi del passato. L'ultimo rintocco risuona nel Regno Unito, dove il ministro della Difesa, Wes Streeting, ha fatto inviare una lettera circolare a ben 100.000 riservisti, ex militari soggetti a richiamo in caso di emergenze, sollecitati a tenersi pronti a fronteggiare un orizzonte di "minacce rafforzate", fra conflitti e crisi geopolitiche internazionali.

Si tratta di un'iniziativa senza precedenti dall'epoca della Guerra Fredda. Il testo, anticipato dal Telegraph prima di essere confermato dal ministro, non elenca i potenziali attori ostili. Ma è evidente il riferimento alla Russia di Vladimir Putin, additata giusto pochi giorni fa - in un'ennesima allerta firmata dal governo e dai servizi segreti interni dell'MI5 - come ipotetica fonte di attacchi e sabotaggi contro aziende militari britanniche impegnate a fornire armi e attrezzature all'Ucraina, sullo sfondo del sostegno assicurato in prima linea da Londra a Kiev nella guerra contro Mosca.

La lettera, co-firmata dai comandanti dell'Esercito di Sua Maestà, della Royal Navy e della Raf, chiede ai destinatari di aggiornare i recapiti, indicare competenze e lavoro attuali e offrirsi volontari per addestramenti ed esercitazioni come la Steadfast Defender della Nato: in programma all'inizio del 2027.

"E' una precauzione sensata e necessaria se, Dio ci scampi, questo Paese si ritrovasse in guerra", ha dichiarato più tardi alla Bbc il titolare della Difesa della compagine laburista di Andy Burnham. "Operiamo in un contesto di minaccia accresciuta", ha argomentato, aggiungendo - nel tentativo di sdrammatizzare l'impatto mediatico della notizia - che "la gente dovrebbe sentirsi rassicurata anziché allarmata". "Vogliamo che la nazione sia vigile, non in allarme", ha insistito.

"Le lettere non preannunciano una mobilitazione", si è affrettato poi a puntualizzare Calvin Bailey, sottosegretario responsabile del dossier dei Veterani. Resta tuttavia, nella retorica dei giornali, il richiamo a un messaggio interpretato dai più come ammonimento a "prepararsi alla guerra". Almeno sulla carta. Tanto più che lo stesso Streeting non ha esitato a lanciarsi al contempo in un elogio dello "spirito patriottico" attribuito al principe Harry, secondogenito di re Carlo III e unico reale della sua generazione ad esser stato inviato in passato su un fronte di guerra vero (quello dell'Afghanistan), che giorni fa s'era detto pronto a indossare di nuovo la divisa dinanzi alla "minaccia russa": arrivando a definirlo "un'autentica risorsa per il nostro Paese".

A rafforzare lo scenario da clima pre-bellico rimbalza intanto l'annuncio parallelo del rinnovo da parte del governo Burnham di un contratto con Babcock, azienda britannica del comparto militare, per la manutenzione dei sottomarini della Royal Navy (unico strumento del limitato potenziale di deterrenza nucleare del Regno), per un ammontare di 8,7 miliardi di sterline. In un quadro nel quale Londra, a dispetto delle posture muscolari, deve peraltro fare i conti con risorse incerte per la difesa e con un esercito ridotto a 73.000 effettivi in servizio attivo: il numero più basso dal tempo delle guerre napoleoniche.

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau military leaders delay presidential election until 2028
articles.summary: Military leaders say presidential and legislative poll scheduled for December 6 will now take place in November 2028.
articles.preview: Military leaders say presidential and legislative poll scheduled for December 6 will now take place in November 2028. Guinea-Bissau’s military leaders have delayed next month’s presidential and legislative election by two years, pushing back a vote that was meant to return the country to civilian rule. A decree issued on Thursday by the transitional president, Major-General Horta Inta-a, said the elections initially scheduled for December 6 would instead take place in November 2028.
articles.body:
Military leaders say presidential and legislative poll scheduled for December 6 will now take place in November 2028.

Guinea-Bissau’s military leaders have delayed next month’s presidential and legislative election by two years, pushing back a vote that was meant to return the country to civilian rule.

A decree issued on Thursday by the transitional president, Major-General Horta Inta-a, said the elections initially scheduled for December 6 would instead take place in November 2028.

The decree said there was “an insufficiency of the technical, material and financial conditions” necessary to hold the vote.

The army seized power in the West African country last November, disrupting a presidential vote and overthrowing the incumbent, Umaro Sissoco Embalo, who was seeking a new term.

The coup inaugurated former army chief of staff Inta-a as head of the military government, tasked with overseeing a one-year transition period.

The transitional charter published in early December barred Inta-a from running for election.

In August, voters approved a constitutional change that gives the president more powers.

Last month, Prime Minister Ilidio Vieira Te said the necessary conditions were not in place for elections in December, though he did not provide a new timeline.

The regional bloc, the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), had called for a short, structured and transparent transition back to civilian rule.

Guinea-Bissau, one of the world’s poorest countries, has been dogged by coups and attempted coups since its independence from Portugal more than 50 years ago.

The country of 2.2 million people is known as a hub for drug trafficking between Latin America and Europe – a trend that experts say has fuelled its political crises.

West Africa has seen a wave of coups since 2020.

articles.title: Los sabotajes que Europa atribuye a Rusia se perfeccionan y disparan el riesgo de “víctimas en masa”
articles.summary: Una investigación del Instituto Internacional de Estudios Estratégicos (IISS) advierte de que la intensidad de esta guerra no convencional aumenta, con el fin de socavar el apoyo a Ucrania y aumentar las divisiones entre los países del continente
articles.preview: Una investigación del Instituto Internacional de Estudios Estratégicos (IISS) advierte de que la intensidad de esta guerra no convencional aumenta, con el fin de socavar el apoyo a Ucrania y aumentar las divisiones entre los países del continente Explosiones en vías de trenes en Polonia, líneas eléctricas dañadas en los países bálticos, incendios en empresas estratégicas o vuelos desviados por amenazas o espacios aéreos temporalmente cerrados.
articles.body:
Una investigación del Instituto Internacional de Estudios Estratégicos (IISS) advierte de que la intensidad de esta guerra no convencional aumenta, con el fin de socavar el apoyo a Ucrania y aumentar las divisiones entre los países del continente

Explosiones en vías de trenes en Polonia, líneas eléctricas dañadas en los países bálticos, incendios en empresas estratégicas o vuelos desviados por amenazas o espacios aéreos temporalmente cerrados. Los sabotajes presuntamente orquestados por Rusia en Europa se intensifican y perfeccionan, con un riesgo cada día mayor de que uno de ellos cause numerosas víctimas, según advierte el Instituto Internacional de Estudios Estratégicos (IISS) en un informe publicado este jueves.

“El uso de explosivos y los incendios provocados se han duplicado en el último año, lo que supone un riesgo de que se produzcan víctimas en masa”, advierte el reconocido grupo de expertos británico. Su informe estima que los actos de sabotaje, que han aumentado un 14% entre octubre de 2025 y septiembre de 2026, tienen por objetivo interrumpir la ayuda militar a Ucrania, pero también sembrar la división en Europa. “El sabotaje aún no ha logrado un golpe de efecto estratégico, pero una sola operación que causara víctimas mortales o una interrupción prolongada de los servicios básicos probablemente pondría de manifiesto las divisiones entre los gobiernos europeos”, advierte el informe.

Por ahora, afirma la institución, Rusia no ha logrado su objetivo, y “no está influyendo sustancialmente en la toma de decisiones en Europa”, ya que la ayuda militar a Ucrania continúa intacta. Pero la pregunta en el aire es si ese apoyo se podrá mantener cuando varios países, empezando por España, y siguiendo por Francia, Polonia, Grecia, Estonia, Finlandia, Italia o Países Bajos celebren elecciones en los próximos meses. En algunos casos, se prevé que las urnas signifiquen un aumento de poder de formaciones de extrema derecha, varias de ellas cercanas al Kremlin.

Alemania y Polonia, los países europeos cuya logística e industria desempeñan un papel fundamental en el apoyo a Ucrania, registran el mayor porcentaje de actos de sabotaje denunciados y atribuidos a Moscú. Más de la mitad de los incidentes registrados entre octubre de 2025 y septiembre pasado tuvieron lugar en esos países, según las conclusiones del informe.

Entre octubre del año pasado y septiembre de este año se registraron en Polonia 29 actos de sabotaje vinculados a Moscú, incluido uno ocurrido en noviembre de 2025 en el que una carga explosiva dañó una línea ferroviaria que sirve para transportar ayuda a Ucrania. No hubo víctimas, pero el primer ministro polaco, Donald Tusk, afirmó posteriormente que era probable que la explosión se hubiera planeado para destruir un tren. “Los ataques contra infraestructuras públicas y lugares de gran repercusión mediática parecen tener como objetivo socavar la confianza y el apoyo de la población a Ucrania”, señala el informe.

Frente a esta guerra silenciosa, según el IISS, los gobiernos europeos han reforzado la protección de las infraestructuras, han tomado medidas para desbaratar las operaciones rusas y limitar las consecuencias de un atentado, pero no han logrado disuadir a los servicios de inteligencia que están detrás. Es decir, han expulsado a agentes de inteligencia, detenido a representantes, cerrado consulados rusos y hasta cambiado leyes en respuesta a incidentes específicos, pero no existe una “estrategia a escala europea que limite la actuación rusa”. “Los miembros europeos de la OTAN se enfrentan a un desafío constante a la hora de adaptar sus esfuerzos individuales y colectivos para disuadir y abortar estas operaciones”, reconoce el informe.

En el caso del ataque con drones en el aeropuerto de Leipzig, en agosto de 2026, el Gobierno alemán tardó un mes en señalar formalmente a Rusia como responsable del ataque y cerrar el consulado de Rusia en Bonn, el único que quedaba en el país, y un centro cultural ruso en Berlín. En el caso del sabotaje de las vías de tren en Polonia, la investigación logró identificar a dos ciudadanos ucranios que colaboran con los servicios secretos rusos y acto seguido cerró el último consulado de Rusia en el país.

La cooperación europea en materia de aplicación de la ley y de inteligencia ha aumentado notablemente en los últimos cuatro años. Pero sigue sin estar claro si las respuestas de Europa están cambiando los cálculos del Kremlin, más allá de hacer que su guerra no convencional resulte más difícil de llevar a cabo. “Los servicios de inteligencia conservan la capacidad de reclutar miembros, están adaptando su enfoque y siguen imponiendo costes, incluso mediante amenazas que perturban los servicios sin causar daños físicos”, se lee en el estudio.

Los líderes políticos europeos han afirmado en repetidas ocasiones que la campaña de guerra híbrida de Rusia se está intensificando. En septiembre pasado, la alta representante para Política Exterior y Seguridad, Kaja Kallas, advirtió de una intensificación de estos ataques. “Debemos estar vigilantes porque vemos informes de inteligencia que dicen que Rusia está planeando más sabotajes, actos y ataques contra nuestra democracia, para dividir nuestra sociedad, intimidarnos para que dejemos de apoyar a Ucrania”, dijo.

Sin embargo, el lenguaje utilizado para describir la guerra no convencional de Rusia contra Europa sigue siendo objeto de controversia, según los autores del informe del IISS. Los líderes europeos se refieren a “amenazas híbridas”, “sabotaje” y “terrorismo de Estado”, términos que reflejan las opiniones divergentes sobre la naturaleza de las acciones de Rusia y sobre cómo debería responder Europa, según los expertos.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Thursday expressed her concern over a Ukrainian drone strike in the Libyan port city of Benghazi against a Russian warship and a cargo vessel.

“You know my support, and the Italian support for Ukraine. But I think that the war should not and cannot be expanded to the Mediterranean. I think that we must be very clear about this,” Meloni, a staunch ally of Ukraine, told reporters.

“I think we must do our best to continue to help Ukraine defend itself, but we must also defend the security of our borders and our citizens, and so I have been and intend to continue to be very clear about this with President Zelenskyy and Ukraine,” she said.

The strike was not the first time Ukraine used Libya to attack Russian vessels.

In March, Ukrainian sea drones struck and badly damaged a Russian-flagged tanker carrying liquefied natural gas near Maltese waters.

Sunday’s attack, however, is a potentially significant escalation in Ukraine’s attacks on Russian interests overseas.

Oil-rich Libya, a former Italian colony, has been mired in chaos since a NATO-backed uprising in 2011 became a civil war that toppled longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi, who was later killed.

For much of the past decade, the country has remained divided between two administrations backed by rival foreign powers.

Libya is strategically important for Italy, connected to the North African country with direct oil and gas undersea pipelines.

Italian oil giant ENI also runs several important fields and terminals in the west of the country.

Il no al Congresso dell'Anm e la risposta di Tango Meloni non andrà al Congresso dell'Associazione nazionale magistrati, in programma da venerdì a domenica a Napoli. "La magistratura associata - ha ricordato Tango - ha fatto un passo verso il dialogo, ma purtroppo ha ricevuto l'ennesimo attacco strumentale, in merito a una sentenza che riguarda l'applicazione di una legge dello Stato. "Ovviamente, non essendo un'ipocrita, se fossi andata al Congresso avrei segnalato questa materia, e quindi sarebbe diventato un attacco - ha poi aggiunto parlando della sua non partecipazione al congresso di Anm -. Non voglio creare questa polemica, quindi il mio passo indietro in realtà è un tentativo di evitare ulteriori polemiche su una questione sulla quale non intendo tornare indietro e non intendo cambiare posizione. Perché non saprei come giustificarlo nei confronti degli italiani, con tutti i problemi che noi abbiamo in questo momento", ha precisato Meloni. "Poiché mi conosco, e non sono una persona che viene e tace quelle che sono le difficoltà, non voglio che poi il giorno dopo si dica che Meloni è venuta al Congresso e ha attaccato. Non voglio attaccare, voglio fare un passo indietro e sperare che ci sia un momento più adeguato per potersi confrontare sullo stato della giustizia. Materia sulla quale sono come sempre molto interessata e attenta", ha concluso.
