articles.body:
Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war.

It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association.

Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights.

“These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. These fissures in the international system are not going to dissolve any time soon.”

Nusseibeh had a setback last Friday, when three permanent members of the UN security council, China, France and the UK, all voted to “discourage” her candidature. The UN’s electoral system requires that she secure nine positive votes from the 15-strong security council, and no discouragement from the permanent five (P5) before being recommended to the UN general assembly.

She has the backing of the US and Russia, and thinks her cause is not lost. “Sometimes, the use of the veto is tactical. Sometimes, it’s a holding position, sometimes it’s a leveraging position. There are a number of different theories”.

The centre of the resistance to Nusseibeh’s candidacy is probably London, and specifically the Foreign Office, the penholder on Sudan at the UN, and this may explain the UK political blitz.

When questioned about her role in Sudan, she asked that her candidacy be seen in the round, highlighting her role in forcing humanitarian aid into Gaza, her support for Afghan women and promoting interfaith tolerance.

“Like every candidate, I come from somewhere, but the independence of the incoming secretary general is the key to their credibility.

“I’ve taken a leave of absence from my role in [the] UAE government in order to independently campaign for this role. But I think that if I was secretary general, Sudan would be the litmus test of success for any incoming secretary because it’s such a horrific humanitarian crisis.”

The war in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between the military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Multiple regional powers, including the UAE, have backed different local proxies since the beginning of the conflict in an attempt to win influence and strategic resources.

The UAE has long been accused of supporting the RSF in Sudan, a charge repeatedly denied by Nusseibeh, who has publicly disputed the findings of UN investigators.

A UN panel of experts suggested last month that the UAE had supplied crucial support to the RSF.

Asked if she regretted dissembling during her time as a diplomat, by denying the UAE had armed the RSF, or her personal role in challenging the UN reports critical of the UAE, Nusseibeh said she regretted that “the Sudanese civil war had continued for so long”.

Nusseibeh added: “But I don’t think saying that is enough for the Sudanese people and the people in the surrounding countries where they’ve also felt the impact of this war, or for the victims of sexual violence and in this conflict, the atrocities committed in El Fasher without accountability, and the use of chemical weapons against the civilian population; all of these are a litany of suffering that has been inflicted on the Sudanese people.”

Asked if the UAE had been supplying weapons to the RSF in a breach of a UN embargo, she replied: “I’m aware of the allegations. I haven’t read the last UN panel of experts report, but I’m not going to comment as I’m no longer a UAE official. In this campaign, I am a secretary general candidate.

“As secretary general, I would fully back the findings of all UN panel of experts reports and I’m aware that I think several countries have been mentioned in various reports.”She later added: “I would call out countries that are supplying arms to any of the parties, including those in the RSF … this needs a process that requires accountability for atrocities that have been committed. That it needs to be a process primarily led by the Sudanese people.”

Nusseibeh said she was willing to take risks to mediate and to put UN values, expertise and its development toolkit at the centre of disputes. Her analysis of contemporary diplomacy was that the world had descended into a default setting of non-cooperation, and the UN needed to restate the case for collaboration between nations as being in the self-interest of everyone.

The UN had been missing from too many conflicts, she argued, and she would set up a mediation board to try to use the full UN toolkit, ranging from confidence-building measures to development to secure peace. “What’s missing is this idea of a secretary general that is a strategist and a mediator-in-chief that is looking at the sort of the blips on the dashboard of conflict and saying, ‘How do we deploy to have maximum impact for most effective use of resource and cost?’ Because resources are not going up, they’re going down. I mean, we’re looking at, since 2010, 40% increase in military spending. So we’re using a lot of hard power as countries and systems to deter, but it’s not actually working.”

That would require some prioritisation at the UN – it has 4,000 different open mandates.

Her intelligence and skills as a diplomat are not in question. However, her track record over Sudan is.

One critic said: “It is a very smart strategic play by the UAE that seeks autocratic capture, and then the asset-stripping of the UN and its standards. The UAE would end the UN’s role on climate. It would be a catastrophe.”

The next security council vote is on Monday. By then some of the backmarkers may have dropped out of the race. The diplomats of the P5 may also be clearer on the flexibility of their mandates, in which case the papal conclave may finally produce white smoke.

articles.title: War in Ukraine: Russia ignores claims on troop casualty figures
articles.summary: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Wednesday declined to comment on claims that around 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the Ukraine war so far.
articles.preview: Russia Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Wednesday declined to comment on claims that around 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the Ukraine war so far. The allegations are based on hacked data from Russia's official statistics agency. After analysing a trove of hacked data from Russia's official statistics agency, several Russian and international media outlets say Moscow's own data shows that between 470,000 and 700,000 soldiers have been killed in the war.
articles.body:
Russia

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Wednesday declined to comment on claims that around 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the Ukraine war so far.

The allegations are based on hacked data from Russia's official statistics agency.

After analysing a trove of hacked data from Russia's official statistics agency, several Russian and international media outlets say Moscow's own data shows that between 470,000 and 700,000 soldiers have been killed in the war.

But Peskov said only the defence ministry can disclose figures and told reporters "not to pay attention to any other data".

"The only entity that can officially disclose casualty figures is the defence ministry of the Russian Federation," he said.

Russia has not given an official death toll among its army since September 2022, when it said almost 6,000 soldiers had been killed in the first six months of fighting — a figure widely seen as a large undercount even at the time.

Earlier this month, hackers from two anti-Kremlin groups — the Belarusian Cyberpartisans and pro-Ukrainian outfit Silent Crow — published hundreds of thousands of records they said had been obtained by hacking the database of Russia's federal statistics agency, Rosstat.

By analysing the unpublished data on causes of death among Russian citizens over the last five years, several international outlets said the data showed the number of soldiers confirmed killed was close to 500,000.

A separate analysis by the banned independent Russian outlets Meduza and Mediazona said after including soldiers classified as "missing" — widely understood to have been killed but not yet registered — the toll could be as high as 700,000.

Significant numbers of Ukrainian soldiers have also been killed in what has become Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II.

articles.title: Se si spengono i satelliti
articles.summary: Da quando è iniziata la guerra in Iran, le immagini satellitari a disposizione dei giornali sono sempre meno e di qualità peggiore
articles.preview: Quando gli Stati Uniti hanno deciso di attaccare l’Iran, lo scorso febbraio, nelle prime ore era emersa la notizia che tra gli obiettivi colpiti dai bombardamenti ci fosse anche una scuola. A dichiararlo erano stati i mezzi d’informazione iraniani, mentre la Reuters, citando due funzionari statunitensi, aveva definito l’attacco “probabile”, ma non certo, e il Pentagono stava ancora indagando sui fatti.
articles.body:
Quando gli Stati Uniti hanno deciso di attaccare l’Iran, lo scorso febbraio, nelle prime ore era emersa la notizia che tra gli obiettivi colpiti dai bombardamenti ci fosse anche una scuola. A dichiararlo erano stati i mezzi d’informazione iraniani, mentre la Reuters, citando due funzionari statunitensi, aveva definito l’attacco “probabile”, ma non certo, e il Pentagono stava ancora indagando sui fatti.

Per raccontare questa notizia, la redazione di un giornale ha due strade: riportare le dichiarazioni ufficiali, avvertendo che si tratta di prime ricostruzioni non ancora verificate, oppure avviare indagini indipendenti per accertare i fatti. Questa seconda strada, nel caso di guerre o disastri naturali, comporta spesso l’utilizzo di immagini satellitari: fotografie che possono aiutare a mostrare la situazione di un territorio prima e dopo un bombardamento, un’alluvione e così via.

Ma proprio a causa della guerra contro l’Iran, le immagini disponibili per questo tipo di verifiche si sono ridotte drasticamente. “Le immagini satellitari sono diventate uno strumento prezioso per il giornalismo visivo”, ha scritto Joseph Clark, giornalista dell’Economist, nella newsletter Off the Charts dello scorso 1 settembre. “Ma le pressioni del governo statunitense sulle aziende che gestiscono i satelliti commerciali hanno rallentato e, in alcuni casi, limitato la diffusione delle immagini della guerra in Iran. Ne hanno risentito ricercatori, redazioni e organizzazioni per i diritti umani, che hanno perso l’accesso a una fonte di informazioni preziosa proprio quando ne avevano più bisogno”.

Di fronte a questo ostacolo, le redazioni hanno cominciato a utilizzare immagini satellitari a risoluzione più bassa, messe a disposizione da enti pubblici come il programma europeo Copernicus, coordinato dall’Agenzia spaziale europea. In alcuni casi, ha spiegato Clark, un’analisi accurata permette alle immagini di Copernicus di restituire informazioni equivalenti a quelle dei satelliti commerciali ad alta risoluzione, con il vantaggio di una maggiore frequenza di acquisizione.

Per esempio, il Conflict Ecology, un gruppo di ricerca dell’Università statale dell’Oregon, ha utilizzato i dati del satellite Sentinel-1, parte del programma Copernicus, per stimare i danni agli edifici provocati dal terremoto in Venezuela. L’Economist ha applicato lo stesso metodo per verificare le distruzioni in Ucraina.

Per il ricercatore Ollie Ballinger, specializzato nell’utilizzo di fonti satellitari aperte, “le aziende che vendono immagini satellitari sono molto sensibili alle pressioni di Washington, perché il governo statunitense è il loro cliente principale”. Queste immagini permetterebbero di documentare proprio ciò che l’amministrazione statunitense preferirebbe tenere nascosto all’opinione pubblica, aggiunge: gli effetti degli attacchi missilistici statunitensi su scuole e abitazioni.

Nei primi giorni della guerra in Iran, le immagini satellitari avevano permesso di ricostruire nel dettaglio gli attacchi missilistici statunitensi contro obiettivi civili. Avevano inoltre mostrato che i danni subiti dalle basi statunitensi erano maggiori di quanto riconosciuto dall’amministrazione di Donald Trump. Ma la Casa Bianca e alcuni parlamentari avevano reagito con preoccupazione, temendo che l’Iran potesse utilizzare le stesse immagini, disponibili sul mercato, per localizzare e colpire i militari statunitensi.

“Negli ultimi anni le dimensioni dei satelliti si sono ridotte”, aggiunge Ballinger, “passando da apparecchi grandi come scuolabus a oggetti delle dimensioni di una scatola da scarpe. Oggi in orbita ce ne sono migliaia, gestiti da aziende di tutto il mondo. Questo significa che, anche con le restrizioni statunitensi, l’Iran può comunque procurarsi le immagini che gli interessano attraverso i satelliti cinesi”.

E, nel frattempo, chi fa ricerca resta “senza un accesso affidabile a quei dati”.

Nessuna elaborazione di immagini a bassa risoluzione può però sostituire la possibilità di individuare eventi che solo i satelliti commerciali ad alta risoluzione riescono a documentare, spiega Joseph Clark, giornalista dell’Economist. È il caso del massacro di Al Fashir, in Darfur, in Sudan, o del conteggio delle persone che si accalcano nei punti di distribuzione degli aiuti a Gaza. Senza immagini ad alta risoluzione, spiega Clark, le persone e le tracce di sangue sulle strade rischierebbero di non essere viste: con la bassa risoluzione si distinguerebbero soltanto pixel sfocati.

Inoltre, anche le immagini gratuite a bassa risoluzione cominciano a essere soggette a limitazioni. A luglio, sempre in seguito a una richiesta del governo statunitense, Copernicus ha ritardato di 24 ore la pubblicazione delle immagini sul golfo di Oman. Finora si tratta di un caso isolato, ma dimostra che nemmeno le immagini satellitari distribuite secondo politiche di accesso aperto sono del tutto affidabili, si legge ancora nella newsletter dell’Economist.

A complicare il lavoro contribuiscono anche le immagini satellitari false generate con l’intelligenza artificiale. Google Earth aveva introdotto uno strumento di questo tipo, poi ritirato dopo le critiche. Henk van Ess, un esperto di fonti aperte che per primo aveva segnalato questi rischi, ha raccontato alla Npr di aver provato a generare immagini di migranti al confine messicano, di una centrale nucleare in Iran, di un incidente ad Amsterdam e di un ospedale con un cratere provocato da una bomba a Gaza. Lo strumento di Google non aveva mai rifiutato di produrle.

Questo testo è tratto dalla newsletter Numeri.

George Quintero, un colonnello in pensione che fa il consulente sulla sicurezza per il governo di Bogotá, ha affermato che l’operazione è opera di uno dei due gruppi armati che si contendono il controllo della zona: l’Esercito di liberazione nazionale (Eln) e il Frente 33, un gruppo dissidente delle Farc.

Secondo il centro studi colombiano Fundación ideas para la paz gli attacchi con droni sono passati da 119 nel 2024 a 351 quest’anno. Sempre il 23 novembre un’autobomba è esplosa nella città di Villavicencio, davanti alla sede del governo del dipartimento di Meta. ◆

articles.body:
Pochi giorni dopo il vertice di Shenzhen del 19 novembre, in cui Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping e Donald Trump hanno ribadito le proprie posizioni senza fare passi avanti verso una soluzione del conflitto, l’Ucraina ha compiuto un’operazione militare nel Mediterraneo. Il 22 novembre sette droni navali hanno attaccato due navi russe nel porto di Bengasi, in Libia, affondando la corvetta Merkury e colpendo il cargo Angara, usato per trasportare armamenti. Il giorno prima un altro attacco aveva danneggiato una nave russa nel golfo di Finlandia. L’operazione in Libia è stata rivendicata dal presidente Volodymyr Zelenskyj, mentre Mosca non ha commentato. La missione di sostegno dell’Onu nel paese ha chiesto un’indagine indipendente. Intanto la Russia continua a bombardare l’Ucraina. In una settimana i russi hanno lanciato 2.770 droni, 165 missili e più di 1.440 bombe plananti, provocando, tra il 21 e il 25 novembre, 18 morti e più di settanta feriti. Zelenskyj ha chiesto a Washington nuovi sistemi di difesa antiaerea, e il 23 novembre la Commissione europea ha proposto un nuovo pacchetto di sanzioni contro Mosca. Basandosi su dati sottratti all’istituto nazionale di statistica russo, i siti Mediazona e Meduza hanno stimato che dall’inizio della guerra sono morti almeno 720mila militari russi.

articles.title: Hamas political official and wife among eight Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza
articles.summary: The killings are the latest from a series of near daily attacks by Israel against what it says are Hamas targets.
articles.preview: A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday. Local sources told the BBC a residential apartment in Deir al-Balah was targeted at dawn, killing Khaled Abu Nada - the deputy education minister - and his wife, Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada. A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman said that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.
articles.body:
A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.

Local sources told the BBC a residential apartment in Deir al-Balah was targeted at dawn, killing Khaled Abu Nada - the deputy education minister - and his wife, Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada.

A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman said that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.

In a joint statement, Israel's prime minister and defence minister said the operation was "part of a series of targeted killings" against Hamas officials.

Thursday's strikes also reportedly killed three Palestinians on al-Nafaq Street, east of Gaza City. Their identities have not yet been established, eyewitnesses said.

In a separate strike on Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, three Palestinians working for Hamas's security services were killed. They were identified as Yasser al-Lahham, Iyad Ahmed and Ibrahim al-Mashal.

In a post X, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the death of Khaled Abu Nada and said about 80 Hamas officials have been killed in the last month.

"No one in Hamas's leadership will succeed in evading us," he said, adding that the military would "continue to pursue our enemies and protect the security of Israeli civilians".

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had carried out a strike on a "senior" Hamas operative, and would provide further details later.

The attacks came a day after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters were killed in Israeli air strike on their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.

On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.

At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,772 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Russia-Ukraine war extends to the Baltic and the Mediterranean
articles.summary: By attacking Russian vessels around the world, Kyiv is trying to up the pressure on Moscow and also sending out signals to its Western allies. What is the impact on global maritime trade?
articles.preview: Russia-Ukraine war extends to the Baltic Sea and the Mediterranean November 26, 2026 By attacking Russian vessels around the world, Kyiv is trying to up the pressure on Moscow and also sending out signals to its Western allies. What is the impact on global maritime trade? First there was an attack on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, off the Finnish coast, then on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel that was allegedly carrying weapons off the coast of Libya.
articles.body:
Russia-Ukraine war extends to the Baltic Sea and the Mediterranean

November 26, 2026

By attacking Russian vessels around the world, Kyiv is trying to up the pressure on Moscow and also sending out signals to its Western allies. What is the impact on global maritime trade?

First there was an attack on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, off the Finnish coast, then on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel that was allegedly carrying weapons off the coast of Libya. These spectacular Ukrainian operations in regions far from the Ukrainian capital Kyiv have caused a stir. They came shortly after several suspected Russian missiles crashed in Poland, not far from where an international military exercise was underway.

Intelligence agencies have long warned that Russia was preparing some form of provocation along NATO's eastern flank.

What are the risks of Russia's war in Ukraine escalating further and drawing in other regions?

It is no secret that Russia has long since expanded its operations beyond Ukraine: With military provocation, hybrid operations and acts of sabotage, Moscow has attempted to put pressure on the countries that openly support Ukraine.

And Ukraine has also targeted Russia's military and economy beyond its borders.

Since the summer, attacks by both Russia and Ukraine have increased in the Black Sea. Not only have Russian and Ukrainian cargo ships been targeted, but also vessels from other countries, particularly Turkey.

Furthermore, in the past few years, Ukraine has managed to deal significant blows to Russia, deep within Russian territory, thanks to aerial and maritime drones. It has targeted military airfields and other strategic targets such as oil refineries, including one in Omsk, Siberia, as well as military vessels in the eastern Black Sea.

Ukrainian attacks in Baltic Sea region

Russia has access only to a very narrow strip of the Baltic Sea coast, which is flanked by Finland and Estonia. Even ahead of the attack on the Sparta II, Ukraine had struck in the area multiple times, targeting oil terminals in the region around St. Petersburg, in Ust-Luga and Primorsk.

Russia uses the Baltic Sea to transport supplies to its Kaliningrad exclave and to export oil and other goods to the rest of the world, with the help of its "shadow fleet."

Ukrainian special forces are also said to have carried out operations against Russian military facilities in Syria, well before the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. They are also reported to have lent support to local Tuareg fighters in Mali who were able to inflict heavy losses on the Malian army and allied Russian mercenaries.

Kyiv is thus attempting to harm Russia's military and economy worldwide, even if in military terms this does not help Ukraine directly.

The Russian corvette that was sunk was part of Russia's Black Sea Fleet but because of Turkey's blockade of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, it would not have been allowed to return to the Black Sea. Instead, it was escorting Russian cargo ships in the Mediterranean. Primarily, the attacks send a political message: Russian ships can no longer feel safe — anywhere in the world.

Could war become omnipresent?

"We are not speaking about random shadow vessels which simply transport oil above the price cap and as a result bring revenues for the Russian treasury," security expert Elisabeth Braw from the Atlantic Council told DW. Sparta II was suspected of carrying military equipment, which Moscow denies.

"Ukraine is showing that it knows exactly, and secondly that it's able to hit them wherever and whatever waters they are in," Braw continued. "And this is something I don't think Ukraine has been able to do at the beginning of the war."

Officially, Kyiv's goal is to disrupt Russian logistics and supply routes, but military experts and politicians also see the attacks as a clear political signal to Western allies. They suspect that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is sending a clear message of strength with an eye toward possible future peace negotiations.

In an interview on the German news outlet Tagesschau, security expert Joachim Weber from the University of Bonn suggested that Zelenskyy was paying less attention to the US, out of a sense of disappointment. He said that Ukrainian attacks in distant maritime areas were a sign that there was less inhibition and that Ukraine was ready to expand the conflict geographically to increase pressure on Russia, despite the risks.

Weber warned that war could become omnipresent if there was an increase in attacks on civilian vessels or ships that were considered suspicious in international waters. He said that Russia was providing more military escorts for the ships of its shadow fleet. "The likelihood that an accidental exchange of fire between armed forces, coast guards or anyone could occur is rising."

Braw pointed out that violations of the Law of the Sea were not only rising with regard to the Russia-Ukraine war but also in relation to other conflicts and playing out in "the South China Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea."

She said about 90% of global trade today was conducted via the oceans and she feared that others might conclude it was not "really to their advantage" to follow the rules of international maritime law.

She added that they might find it "beneficial in the short term to violate maritime rules" for short-term gains. "That would make the world's oceans significantly less safe for everybody."

Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going.

articles.title: Is Alice Huang a spy or not?
articles.summary: The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed exec with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair, is a Chinese spy.
articles.preview: The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, a former executive at the data-center company Megaspeed, is a Chinese spy. She had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who abruptly resigned on Nov. 12 after acknowledging it and was just as abruptly reinstated on Monday of this week. What’s publicly known is murkier than the headlines suggest. U.S.
articles.body:
The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, a former executive at the data-center company Megaspeed, is a Chinese spy. She had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who abruptly resigned on Nov. 12 after acknowledging it and was just as abruptly reinstated on Monday of this week.

What’s publicly known is murkier than the headlines suggest. U.S. intelligence has reportedly tracked Alice Huang’s contact with an officer of China’s spy agency, but officials haven’t offered public evidence that she was commissioned to target Nvidia’s chief. In the past week, after President Trump successfully pushed to bring Jensen Huang back, the administration has played down the allegations it once circulated internally. Whether that reflects new intelligence or political pressure is the big question.

Undisputed reporting shows the claim emerged from the White House itself. It first appeared in a highly classified memo written in March under the oversight of Secretary of State Marco Rubio and circulated to White House officials ahead of Trump’s trip to China in May. The memo formed the partial basis for the New York Times’ initial reporting on the scandal, published Oct. 29 and its existence was first reported on Nov. 8.

The memo did not definitively say, according to the Wall Street Journal, that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. CNN, by contrast, has reported that the memo concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

What’s better established is that Alice Huang was in touch with Chinese intelligence. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) is Beijing’s civilian spy agency, responsible for both foreign intelligence and domestic counterintelligence. Last weekend, the Times, citing people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports, reported that Huang was in contact with an MSS officer from the spring of 2025 until this fall, a period that overlaps her relationship with Jensen Huang. (The Chinese government has called the spy claims a “smear,” and Megaspeed says Huang left the company in August 2025 and that its business is legitimate.)

Top Trump officials have nonetheless all but discredited the espionage claims, along with the suggestion that Nvidia fell prey to spying or foreign influence.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, who was Trump’s personal defense lawyer before taking over the Justice Department, told journalists on Tuesday: “I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.” On the same day, Trump said a pardon was an option for Jensen Huang but that he did not think one would be needed. Senior intelligence officials reportedly told Congress that the government apparently has no actual evidence that the MSS directed Alice Huang to pursue an affair with Jensen Huang.

None of those statements necessarily exonerates Alice Huang as an intelligence agent. Instead, they support the alternate theory that the Chinese government didn’t tell her to begin the affair and that Jensen Huang broke no law by having it. Not being directed to have an affair isn’t the same as not being a spy, though.

From a certain angle, the circumstantial evidence surrounding Alice Huang looks quite suspicious. She was a top executive at a company investigated for illicitly channeling Nvidia chips to China, and her husband, Kang Wei, is said to have even closer ties to the MSS, with some sources saying he worked for the agency.

The timing of the government’s reversal is at the heart of the matter. Trump has said he lobbied the board “directly and indirectly” to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, so it wouldn’t be surprising if officials who serve at his pleasure were recasting the case in terms that satisfy his agenda. That wouldn’t necessarily make their assessments wrong. But unless new intelligence has actually resolved the question, and none has been publicly identified as yet, that backdrop is critical to keep in mind. CBS has also reported that Rubio, whose office oversaw the original memo, has privately voiced concerns about aspects of Jensen Huang’s return.

Doubts persist elsewhere, too. Earlier this month, CNN reported that the intelligence community was still working to understand Alice Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang and that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove she was acting as a spy for Beijing. After a briefing by top intelligence officials earlier this month, Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, said he was unsure whether she was a spy or a “useful idiot.” And this week, the Wall Street Journal pointed out that under Chinese leader Xi Jinping, top corporate executives routinely maintain ties to the country’s intelligence service without being formally deputized as assets.

The crush of conflicting claims, most from anonymous government sources, obviously leaves large questions unanswered as to what actually transpired. Some of those questions that naturally spring to mind:

- Alice Huang is said to have been under U.S. surveillance for over a year. If the government suspected her of espionage, why wasn’t Jensen Huang warned earlier (and privately, so as not to cause the stock-market-destabilizing maelstrom that followed the more recent disclosure)? One explanation that has been given is that alerting the Nvidia chief might have tipped off Huang that her cover had been blown.

- If Alice Huang was a spy, what information did she pass to the Chinese government, and what influence did she actually have?

- Most critically, how did the allegation reach the public at all? The likeliest answer is a leak. A source told CNN that Rubio briefed Trump on the intelligence in May, yet Trump has since said he only recently learned of the concerns, and in October he presented Jensen Huang with the National Medal of Science. Officials who felt they could not get through to the president may have turned to reporters instead, which would explain how the contents of a memo whose existence has never been disputed found their way into print. What remains unclear is who leaked it, and whether they anticipated the fallout.

There are answers to all of these questions, of course, but when the public will get them is anybody’s guess. Jensen Huang is due to appear before the Senate Banking Committee next week, and by the look from the statements of some of its members, he’s likely in for a rough ride. Unfortunately, congressional hearings, particularly public ones, rarely unearth secrets that haven’t already been disclosed.

articles.title: Android app developers will soon have to share their address publicly
articles.summary: Independent Android app developers are worried about their privacy after Google announced that from next year many of them will be required to share a phone number and address publicly. The policy change is intended to meet European Union regulations under the Digital Services Act, but Google says contact details will be made public worldwide.
articles.preview: Independent Android app developers are worried about their privacy after Google announced that from next year many of them will be required to share a phone number and address publicly. The policy change is intended to meet European Union regulations under the Digital Services Act, but Google says contact details will be made public worldwide.
articles.body:
Independent Android app developers are worried about their privacy after Google announced that from next year many of them will be required to share a phone number and address publicly. The policy change is intended to meet European Union regulations under the Digital Services Act, but Google says contact details will be made public worldwide.

The change is to meet EU regulations, but Apple gives its developers more privacy.

Developers have until February 1st 2027 to declare whether or not they’re a “trader” under UK and European law. Broadly speaking, Google says the definition applies if you earn revenue from your apps, especially if that revenue is regular or at high volume. Developers are exempt if their apps are only a hobby or non-commercial, or if they simply don’t publish them in the UK or Europe.

If they self-declare as a trader, developers’ contact details will be shared publicly starting March 1st, including a phone number and address. Google doesn’t accept PO boxes for developer payment profile addresses, meaning many independent developers without an office will either have to share their home address online or pay for a registered agent or other service that provides a business address. One independent developer told The Elec they were considering renting a private office solely to comply with the new rules. We’ve asked Google to confirm why developers aren’t permitted to publish a PO box address, and why details are being shared globally, and will update this article when we hear back.

Apple is subject to the same regulations, but is handling them differently to Google. It will only display developer addresses within the relevant European countries, rather than publishing them worldwide. It’s also allowing developers to supply PO box addresses, so long as they provide Apple with a receipt or bill that links the PO box to their regular address.

Update, November 26th: Added mention of developers’ option to use a registered agent service for a business address.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue
articles.summary: On the same day that Anthropic entered the public market, a painstakingly human video game became one of most successful entertainment launches of all time.
articles.preview: It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype. Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week. GTA VI launched as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ($2 billion).
articles.body:
It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype. Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week.

GTA VI launched as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ($2 billion).

The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI.

Even the biggest workaholics among us – startup founders – scheduled time off to play the game, including Spiry co-founder Dima Beseda, who told TechCrunch, “I reshuffled my workload to free up time around the weekends and even booked vitamin IV drips to keep my energy up.”

Yet some players felt a sense of anticipatory nostalgia as they wiped away a layer of dust on their Xbox to play the game they’d been looking forward to since they were kids.

“We do have a view that GTA is likely to be the last game of its kind to be made this way,” Ben Feder, managing partner at TIRTA Ventures and former CEO of Rockstar parent company Take-Two Interactive, told TechCrunch.

That’s because GTA VI was created entirely without generative AI.

“We’re kind of at this technological moment where this way of developing has sort of reached its natural frontier,” Feder said. “I don’t think you can say that games like this will always be around.”

As millions of people immersed themselves in Vice City, the tech industry witnessed another long-awaited moment: Anthropic became the first major AI lab to go public. At Nasdaq HQ, Anthropic executives gathered to celebrate the Claude maker’s $81.3 billion IPO. At virtually the same moment that Anthropic broke the record for the largest IPO ever, GTA VI was also breaking records with the highest-rated and best-selling game launch of all time.

But when the Anthropic team rang the bell on Thursday, the sound also signaled the end of an era in video game development, and perhaps even in the arts at large.

The AI industry operates with efficiency as its north star. The promise of this technology is that we will be able to automate so much work that we can expand the capabilities of humanity, avoiding needless time spent tinkering with ultimately fruitless ideas. Instead, a prompt goes into an LLM, and a response is spat out.

This technological revolution exploded into the world with some soul-crushing side effects: children are inundated with mind-numbing slop on YouTube, lawyers cite nonexistent cases in court, and tech companies like Meta lay off tens of thousands of people as part of a corporate-branded “Year of Efficiency.” But against the backdrop of the AI industry’s first major IPO, Rockstar has unveiled a game that about 5,000 people labored over for more than a decade.

The final product is breathtaking, looking so lifelike that it can be hard to distinguish gameplay footage from real life. These sprawling open-world games are usually made possible by procedurally generating new landscapes and objects, but Rockstar has taken the time to painstakingly craft every detail of the world, even developing 30,000 different nonplayable characters with unique appearances and personalities.

The video game industry is already grappling with the threat of AI. Google’s Project Genie, which launched earlier this year, allows users to create and wander around 3D worlds generated from prompts to an LLM. The stock prices of several video game companies faltered around the time of Project Genie’s release, perhaps because of investors’ uncertainty about the future relevance of video game developers.

“The notion that somehow new tools would allow an individual to push a button and generate a hit, market a hit, and bring it to many millions of consumers around the world, it’s a laughable notion,” Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said at the time. “It’s just never been the case with entertainment.”

Zelnick’s fellow tech CEOs see different future, though. On a Meta earnings call this year, CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised that, “soon, you’ll have an AI that understands you and [can] even generate great personalized content for you.”

Elon Musk even went as far as proposing that a game like GTA VI could be made with AI.

“You won’t even have to ask,” Musk wrote on X. “AI will figure what video game you’d like best.”

This is the paradox of “Grandthropic” week. GTA VI is so impressively vast and captivating because its developers could make mistakes, experiment, and rework ideas, even if that meant delaying the game (twice). GTA VI was incubated with the exact inefficiencies that investors hope AI companies like Anthropic can help eradicate.

“Plenty of fantastic art — video games and elsewhere — almost by definition has to be created slowly, and there’s something to having that kind of inefficiency around it,” Feder said. “Creative output requires deletion, right? Getting to kind of a masterpiece oftentimes requires an enormous amount of deletion. And when you’re talking about a game of the kind of complexity we’re talking about, that kind of deletion ends up being very expensive, and it is by definition not efficient.”

GTA VI reeks of its own humanity – every small detail is loaded with intention, but it’s this impressive precision that keeps the world abuzz, triggering the kind of monocultural moment that has become increasingly rare in a media landscape that revolves around highly personalized social media algorithms.

The game forces the player to slow down, which is either frustrating or genius, depending on your sense of humor. People waited more than three presidential terms for the next installment in a high-octane action franchise, only to download a 212 GB behemoth of a game in which your earliest missions involve driving around doing errands and putting up drywall to make your girlfriend happy. Don’t worry — there are still car chases and shootouts — but in a moment when AI feels suffocating, GTA VI is such an artistic achievement that it is reaching audiences that don’t even like violent video games.

The ultimate fantasy of GTA VI is no longer to role-play as a criminal — the fantasy is just taking your time to relish the mundane and explore an expansive world that developers were given the time and space to perfect.

articles.preview: Mia figlia fa il primo liceo e, come molti coetanei, usa quotidianamente l’intelligenza artificiale: come si fa a convincerla a fare i compiti da sola quando ha una soluzione così facile a portata di mano?–Liliana Credo che prima di convincere gli studenti a cambiare le loro abitudini dovremmo convincere la scuola a cambiare le proprie.
articles.body:
Mia figlia fa il primo liceo e, come molti coetanei, usa quotidianamente l’intelligenza artificiale: come si fa a convincerla a fare i compiti da sola quando ha una soluzione così facile a portata di mano?–Liliana

Credo che prima di convincere gli studenti a cambiare le loro abitudini dovremmo convincere la scuola a cambiare le proprie. L’Estonia sta facendo un esperimento con ventimila studenti e cinquemila insegnanti: invece di vietare l’uso dell’intelligenza artificiale, si è deciso d’integrarla nell’insegnamento, distinguendo le attività in cui favorisce l’apprendimento da quelle in cui rischia di comprometterlo. Agli studenti è stato fornito un chatbot progettato per comportarsi come un bravo insegnante: se gli sottoponi un problema di matematica, anziché risolverlo ti aiuta a trovare la soluzione. Da un’indagine condotta per il progetto è emerso che sono gli stessi studenti a chiedere regole più chiare sull’uso dell’intelligenza artificiale, perché alcuni si lamentano di prendere voti più bassi dei compagni che la usano. In attesa dei risultati definitivi di questa sperimentazione, l’intelligenza artificiale potrebbe dare nuova attualità a un’idea che molti insegnanti sperimentano da tempo, la classe capovolta. Finora si è chiesto agli alunni di ascoltare le spiegazioni in classe e di fare da soli gli esercizi il pomeriggio. Forse è ora di invertire lo schema: le spiegazioni si possono seguire a casa, con videolezioni o materiali preparati dagli insegnanti, mentre la fatica mentale degli esercizi, di ragionare e scrivere, andrebbe fatta in classe, sotto i loro occhi.

articles.title: La quotazione di Anthropic ha reso ricche molte persone
articles.summary: Molte nel senso di migliaia, ricche nel senso di milionarie
articles.preview: Molte nel senso di migliaia, ricche nel senso di milionarie Dopo la quotazione in borsa di questo mese, le stime dicono che dentro Anthropic ci siano circa seicento persone con azioni dal valore superiore ai cento milioni di dollari. In generale, quasi tutti i dipendenti dell’azienda (il 96 per cento su un totale di 5.300) hanno adesso un patrimonio azionario superiore al milione di dollari, che per poco più della metà di loro (2.800) supera i dieci milioni di dollari.
articles.body:
Molte nel senso di migliaia, ricche nel senso di milionarie

Dopo la quotazione in borsa di questo mese, le stime dicono che dentro Anthropic ci siano circa seicento persone con azioni dal valore superiore ai cento milioni di dollari. In generale, quasi tutti i dipendenti dell’azienda (il 96 per cento su un totale di 5.300) hanno adesso un patrimonio azionario superiore al milione di dollari, che per poco più della metà di loro (2.800) supera i dieci milioni di dollari.

La quotazione in borsa (o IPO) di Anthropic è stata la più grande della storia e ha portato un’azienda fondata poco meno di sei anni fa a raggiungere i 1.500 miliardi di capitalizzazione di mercato (la somma del valore di tutte le sue azioni), creando enorme ricchezza per molti dei suoi investitori e dipendenti. Per l’anno prossimo è prevista anche l’IPO di OpenAI, l’altra grande azienda del settore, che è già stata valutata circa 1.250 miliardi di dollari e potrebbe trasformare in milionari altre migliaia di persone.

Il meccanismo non è di per sé nuovo: a cambiare è semmai la dimensione dei capitali in gioco. La storia del settore tecnologico è fatta di vicende simili, in cui piccole startup finiscono per raggiungere una valutazione altissima e, una volta quotate in borsa, arricchiscono non solo i loro investitori e fondatori, ma anche molti dipendenti che detengono piccole quote. Un caso celebre è quello dell’artista David Choe, che nel 2005 realizzò dei graffiti per la sede di Facebook, accettando di farsi pagare in azioni della neonata azienda: quando questa si quotò in borsa sette anni dopo, le azioni ricevute da Choe valevano circa 200 milioni di dollari.

Come molte startup, Anthropic riconosce ai suoi dipendenti una parte del loro compenso sotto forma di azioni o stock option (il diritto di acquistare azioni a un prezzo deciso in anticipo e quindi potenzialmente minore di quello di mercato). Al momento dell’IPO, alcuni dipendenti di Anthropic hanno potuto vendere subito parte delle loro azioni, mentre gli altri dovranno attendere alcuni mesi (il cosiddetto lock-up). Nel frattempo possono spesso ottenere prestiti usando come garanzia le proprie azioni.

Un discorso a parte vale per i cofondatori di Anthropic, le sette persone che nel 2021 abbandonarono OpenAI, considerata troppo spericolata nello sviluppo di AI, per fondare una nuova azienda. Data la particolare struttura societaria di Anthropic, a loro spetta buona parte del controllo della società, oltre che il 10 per cento circa delle azioni: ciascuno di loro ora ha un patrimonio azionario intorno ai venti miliardi di dollari.

Secondo PitchBook Data, un’azienda che raccoglie dati sulle imprese del settore, a San Francisco si concentra più di un terzo degli investimenti globali di venture capital (quelli ad alto rischio nelle aziende giovani e ancora in perdita), nonostante sia una città relativamente piccola, con circa 800mila abitanti.

La maggior parte di questi soldi è destinata ad aziende che si occupano di AI: oggi in città hanno sede almeno tremila startup del settore – tra cui Anthropic –, che dall’inizio del 2025 hanno ricevuto investimenti per poco meno di 400 miliardi di dollari. Sommando tutte le quote detenute dagli addetti ai lavori di San Francisco nel settore delle AI, si raggiungono i 1.200 miliardi di dollari, secondo una stima di Bloomberg Businessweek.

Si tratta ovviamente di cifre legate alle valutazioni attuali, che potrebbero subire variazioni a seconda dell’andamento del mercato (il titolo di Anthropic è sceso in pochi giorni sotto al valore dell’IPO). Tuttavia, la valutazione dell’azienda – e in generale di tutto il settore delle AI – rimane altissima.

L’improvvisa creazione di migliaia di nuovi milionari con l’IPO di Anthropic sta mettendo ulteriore pressione sul mercato immobiliare di San Francisco, già da tempo tra i più cari degli Stati Uniti. Nel corso dell’ultimo anno, la ricchezza generata dall’AI ha contribuito a far salire il prezzo mediano delle case unifamiliari del 29 per cento (oggi è di 2,39 milioni di dollari), secondo dati citati dal Wall Street Journal. La quotazione di Anthropic rischia di peggiorare la situazione, sia perché molti dei suoi dipendenti vivono e lavorano in città, sia perché anche il resto degli acquirenti ha fretta di concludere le trattative prima che il prezzo aumenti ancora.

Sarah Chieng, dirigente di Cerebras, un’azienda del settore, ha notato su X come la relativa semplicità e velocità con cui una persona può diventare milionaria in questo ambito stia «stravolgendo il rapporto che un’intera generazione ha con soldi, ambizione, lavoro e successo: quando i tuoi coetanei stanno costruendo patrimoni generazionali prima dei 25 anni, che senso ha ormai parlare di una carriera lavorativa normale?».

articles.title: Accordo per De Cos alla Bce, ma è muro contro muro sul bilancio Ue
articles.summary: Via libera dei 27 allo spagnolo. Resta lo scontro tra modernizzatori e coesionisti
articles.preview: L'Europa chiude la (scontata) partita delle nomine al vertice della Banca Centrale, ma si divide sulle risorse con cui finanziare le sue ambizioni per il prossimo settennato. Con il via libera dei leader dell'Eurozona allo spagnolo Pablo Hernandez de Cos per la successione a Christine Lagarde, alla francese Laurence Boone e al tedesco Markus Brunnermeier per il Comitato esecutivo, prende forma la nuova geografia del potere all'Eurotower.
articles.body:
L'Europa chiude la (scontata) partita delle nomine al vertice della Banca Centrale, ma si divide sulle risorse con cui finanziare le sue ambizioni per il prossimo settennato. Con il via libera dei leader dell'Eurozona allo spagnolo Pablo Hernandez de Cos per la successione a Christine Lagarde, alla francese Laurence Boone e al tedesco Markus Brunnermeier per il Comitato esecutivo, prende forma la nuova geografia del potere all'Eurotower. L'intesa vale come brezza fresca in una stanza altrimenti soffocata dall'aria stantia: l'accordo sul bilancio comunitario 2028-2034, infatti, è ancora in alto mare. "Arriverà, come per magia si trova la quadra ogni volta", sottolinea un alto funzionario Ue. Come e quando, resta da vedere.

Ma torniamo alla Bce. La Spagna conquista per la prima volta una delle poltrone più importanti dell'organigramma europeo con l'ex governatore centrale, oggi direttore generale della Banca dei regolamenti internazionali di Basilea. Se il bomber viene da Madrid, le due ali le mettono Parigi e Berlino: l'ex ministra francese per gli Affari europei Boone avrà la responsabilità delle operazioni di mercato, mentre l'economista di Princeton Brunnermeier è destinato all'incarico di capoeconomista. Per il candidato olandese escluso, Klaas Knot, a fine 2027 potrebbe ora aprirsi un'altra partita, quando scadrà il mandato del direttore generale del Mes (l'ipotesi circola a Bruxelles ma il dossier non sarebbe già collegato).

Il premier spagnolo Pedro Sanchez, impegnato nella volata della campagna elettorale dato che le urne si apriranno domenica, ha esultato per la soddisfazione: "Una Spagna che guida l'Europa come non aveva mai fatto". Un risultato non da poco, soprattutto considerando che non è nemmeno presente al Consiglio Europeo (lo rappresenta Emmanuel Macron). Per le nomine formali in Bce restano ora da acquisire i pareri del Parlamento europeo e del Consiglio direttivo dell'Eurotower, col sigillo previsto al summit di dicembre.

Ecco, le buone notizie finiscono qui. Non che non si sapesse.

Il vertice extra è stato disegnato per fallire, in modo da spingere i leader a mettersi d'accordo entro Natale rispettando così la deadline fissata dal presidente Costa, prima che l'Ue venga travolta dal giro di elezioni del 2027, Francia in testa.

Ma neppure su questo c'è concordia. Diverse capitali considerano la tagliola del primo gennaio come artificiale. Le posizioni sono talmente distanti, d'altra parte, che al momento appare impossibile rispettare il cronoprogramma. Costa ha tagliato del 10% la proposta originale della Commissione arrivando al numero totale di 1.582,5 miliardi. Per il campo dei modernizzatori - conta sette capitali ed è capitanato dalla Germania - è ancora troppo e serve scendere. Sulla sponda opposta ci sono gli Amici della Coesione (praticamente tutti gli altri) schierati per un bilancio più "ambizioso" ma soprattutto rispettoso delle priorità tradizionali dell'Ue, come la politica agricola e appunto la riduzione delle disuguaglianze tra le regioni d'Europa. I sette invece vorrebbero puntare su priorità più pressanti per il mondo di oggi, come competitività e difesa.

Ebbene, in questo esercizio complicatissimo i veti volano, ma ciascuno si tiene ben stretto l'asso nella manica, la carta da giocare per chiudere la partita. La particolarità del vertice sono i confessionali: gli incontri tra Costa, Ursula von der Leyen, e i vari Paesi divisi per raggruppamenti. Hanno debuttato i modernizzatori, seguiti dai 'coesionisti'. Quindi gli E6: Germania, Francia, Italia, Paesi Bassi e Spagna (giudicato il più rappresentativo). È in queste sessioni che si negozierà davvero e solo alla fine Costa capirà se si è vicini alla svolta e vale la pena d'insistere col secondo giorno di vertice, oppure è meglio aggiornare a dicembre.

Come se non bastasse, c'è il nodo del finanziamento da 45 miliardi all'Ucraina per il 2027. Il cancelliere Merz lo ha legato all'accordo generale sul bilancio, per spingere i Paesi riottosi a contribuire (Ungheria, Slovacchia, Repubblica Ceca e Bulgaria) ad accodarsi. C'è uno spiraglio. L'ipotesi è di creare due 'buste' separate dentro quei 45 miliardi, una per le spese militari e l'altra per le esigenze civili. Son cavilli, ma utili per domare le proprie opinioni pubbliche.

articles.body:
Spazio su due piani: è il punto vendita numero 222. La Germania è il prossimo mercato strategico

Legami, insegna italiana di regalistica e cartoleria, ha aperto a Milano, in piazza San Babila, la sua più grande boutique a livello internazionale: oltre 450 metri quadrati distribuiti su due piani, in uno snodo urbano strategico, tra l’area pedonale dello shopping milanese e il quadrilatero della moda, a pochi passi da Piazza Duomo. Con questa apertura salgono a 17 i negozi nell’area metropolitana di Milano, città d’elezione del brand.

Questo flagship store è il 222esimo negozio nel mondo per Legami, e rientra nel piano di sviluppo che, fa sapere l’azienda, prevede «numerose nuove aperture nei prossimi anni, sia in Italia sia all’estero». Il brand è oggi presente con i propri punti vendita in Italia, Francia e Spagna, affiancati da una rete di oltre 13.000 rivenditori in più di 70 Paesi, tra cui la Germania, mercato strategico dove nei prossimi mesi verranno aperte le prime boutique dirette del brand.

Tornando alla boutique di piazza San Babila, a Milano, al primo piano i visitatori troveranno 15 penne cancellabili alte due metri, divenute, con i loro personaggi, un simbolo del marchio. La novità qui è un’area dedicata alla personalizzazione, con il proprio nome o un messaggio, di alcuni prodotti come penne, borracce, fino ad agende e notebook. In una teca in vetro, invece, è custodita la collezione storica con tutte le 94 erasable pen, dalle prime del 2018 fino alle edizioni più recenti.

Fondata nel 2003 da Alberto Fassi, Legami conta oggi oltre 5.000 prodotti organizzati in 17 categorie: dalla cancelleria agli accessori per la casa, dagli essenziali per il viaggio agli articoli per la bellezza, passando per giochi vintage e accessori tech.

articles.title: Trump calls GDP data released before midterms ‘fake’, demands investigation
articles.summary: President says it was a deliberate decision to release 'fake' growth numbers before US midterm elections.
articles.preview: President says it was a deliberate decision to release ‘fake’ growth numbers before US midterm elections. United States President Donald Trump has accused his Department of Commerce of purposely issuing incorrect economic growth figures before the midterm elections and says he wants to launch an investigation. Trump made his comments on Thursday when offices and stock markets were closed for the Thanksgiving holiday.
articles.body:
President says it was a deliberate decision to release ‘fake’ growth numbers before US midterm elections.

United States President Donald Trump has accused his Department of Commerce of purposely issuing incorrect economic growth figures before the midterm elections and says he wants to launch an investigation.

Trump made his comments on Thursday when offices and stock markets were closed for the Thanksgiving holiday.

The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis on Wednesday revised third-quarter annualised growth up to 4.3 percent from the advance estimate of 3.4 percent it announced on October 29. Trump’s Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the November 3 elections.

“It was just revealed that the REAL Numbers on the Economy, published before the Election, were FAKE,” Trump said in a Truth Social post without providing evidence for the accusation.

“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation. This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error,” he said.

Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine trust in economic data that fail to match his claims of a historic boom, a pattern that threatens the credibility of figures needed by businesses, financial markets and consumers when making investments.

The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) routinely updates its economic data to improve their accuracy. Gross domestic product (GDP) figures, monthly jobs reports and other data are regularly revised. Those updates occur on a prescheduled basis without regard to the political calendar.

The BEA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It has previously said GDP estimates can differ from the final numbers because advance estimates for quarterly growth lack complete source data on inventories, trade and consumer spending on services.

A May article coauthored by BEA Director Vipin Arora found that for GDP, the estimates released 90 days after initial estimates typically differed by 0.52 percentage points throughout this century.

“That is, over these 25 years, more complete source data expanded or contracted BEA’s estimates of real GDP growth on average by about half a percentage point per quarter,” wrote Arora and coauthor Rebecca Pocase.

Last year, Trump fired a top Department of Labor official after a weak jobs report, accusing her without evidence of manipulating the figures, a move that added to already growing concerns about the quality of economic data published by the federal government.

articles.title: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos wins race to be next ECB president
articles.summary: Former Bank of Spain governor chosen to succeed Christine Lagarde after winning support of EU’s biggest countries Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos has been chosen as the next president of the European Central Bank, to succeed Christine Lagarde, after winning support from the EU’s biggest countries. The economist and monetary policymaker will become the first Spaniard to lead the ECB, defeating his rival candidate Klaas Knot, the former head of the Dutch central bank. Continue reading...
articles.preview: Former Bank of Spain governor chosen to succeed Christine Lagarde after winning support of EU’s biggest countries Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos has been chosen as the next president of the European Central Bank, to succeed Christine Lagarde, after winning support from the EU’s biggest countries. The economist and monetary policymaker will become the first Spaniard to lead the ECB, defeating his rival candidate Klaas Knot, the former head of the Dutch central bank. Continue reading...
articles.body:
Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos has been chosen as the next president of the European Central Bank, to succeed Christine Lagarde, after winning support from the EU’s biggest countries.

The economist and monetary policymaker will become the first Spaniard to lead the ECB, defeating his rival candidate Klaas Knot, the former head of the Dutch central bank.

EU diplomats agreed two other appointments to the ECB’s executive board on Thursday: France’s Laurence Boone and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier. The trio of appointments was a package deal, after France and Germany converged on choosing Hernández de Cos, who is expected to keep the ECB on the same path.

Following the talks European Council president António Costa confirmed the three appointments, saying: “This will pave the way for the formal appointment of the new ECB leadership by the EUCO [European Council] in December.”

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, also confirmed: “A consensus emerged on the nominations to the European Central Bank.”

The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, who faces elections this weekend that he is predicted to lose, celebrated the victory of Hernández de Cos and the presence of Spaniards in other big EU roles, by hailing “a Spain that is leading in Europe as never before”.

Spain’s former deputy prime minister Teresa Ribera is one of the European Commission’s executive vice-presidents, with responsibility for a vast portfolio spanning the green transition and EU competition policy. The former Spanish economy minister Nadia Calviño leads the European Investment Bank.

Hernández de Cos, a former Bank of Spain governor, will become the fifth head of the eurozone’s central bank since it was founded in 1998. He is expected to take up his position after Lagarde stands down in February, during a time of political change and economic pressure in the 21-country eurozone.

Europe is entering a big election year, starting with Spain’s elections this weekend, with national votes to follow in France, Italy and (non-eurozone) Poland. European economies are under growing pressure from fierce Chinese competition, US tariff threats and soaring energy prices that are driving up inflation, as well as high debt in several member states.

One of his biggest challenges will be reining in surging prices: inflation in the eurozone hit 4% last month, up from 2.1% a year earlier.

Hernández de Cos, who is now serving as general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, is seen as supporting lower interest rates to boost growth.

Market analysts are closely watching what Hernández de Cos might say about France, where an embattled minority government is struggling to pass a budget. French debt is forecast to hit 122% of GDP next year, more than twice the limit allowed under EU fiscal rules.

Arne Petimezas, the director of research at AFS Group Amsterdam, said Hernández de Cos, who “leans dovish”, was the “continuity candidate”. He added: “Don’t expect de Cos to turn a blind eye to France and its fiscal predicaments. No carte blanche: bond buying will remain contingent on austerity and a path towards a lower debt ratio.”

The ECB’s approach to the French debt crisis will come under intense political scrutiny, especially after calls from the French far-right presidential frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, “to ease the burden of interest rates”.

Hernández de Cos is seen as a central banker in the mould of Mario Draghi, the celebrated former ECB president and Italian prime minister, who is credited with stabilising the eurozone at a pivotal moment in the debt crisis. Matthew Ryan, at the financial services firm Ebury, said Hernández de Cos was “likely to place greater weight on growth, financial stability and fragmentation risk than Klaas Knot, the alternative candidate and a genuine hawk”.

“We do not expect his appointment to alter the near-term rate path. The president sets the agenda but is ultimately one voice on the governing council, and rarely overrides the consensus.”

The contest was set in motion less than a month ago when Lagarde, the ECB’s first female president, announced that she intended to leave her post nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront “the misrepresentation of the truth”.

Macron, who played a decisive role in appointing Lagarde, a former French finance minister, said EU leaders had welcomed her “decisive leadership during her term in office”.

Hernández de Cos’s appointment must still clear the European parliament and the ECB’s governing council, but these steps are seen as formalities.

È l’economia degli eventi, nota al pubblico degli specialisti come live communication, che continua a macinare numeri positivi, nonostante le incertezze dello scenario internazionale e una maggiore prudenza delle imprese negli investimenti in comunicazione.
articles.body:
Il mercato cresce del +6,7%, ma costi e burocrazia frenano la competitività. A Venezia duemila professionisti da più di 40 Paesi per disegnare il futuro del settore

Nell’epoca delle relazioni mediate dagli algoritmi cresce il valore di quelle costruite dal vivo. È l’economia degli eventi, nota al pubblico degli specialisti come live communication, che continua a macinare numeri positivi, nonostante le incertezze dello scenario internazionale e una maggiore prudenza delle imprese negli investimenti in comunicazione. In Italia il mercato raggiunge quest’anno un valore stimato di un miliardo e 198 milioni di euro, in crescita del +6,7% rispetto all’anno precedente. I numeri sono stati presentati al Lido di Venezia, dove fino al 27 novembre si svolge la Live Communication Week promossa da ADC Group in collaborazione con Next Group e con la partnership di Vela. Alla kermesse stanno partecipando oltre duemila professionisti provenienti da più di 40 Paesi del mondo.

Le prospettive

All’orizzonte si profila un nuovo record storico: entro il 2028 il comparto potrebbe raggiungere 1 miliardo e 306 milioni di euro, con un incremento del +9% e superando il primato di 1,3 miliardi registrato nel 2008. È la fotografia scattata dalla nuova edizione del Monitor sugli eventi e sulla live communication realizzato da AstraRicerche per ADC Group, con il patrocinio di Italian Exhibition Group su un campione di 341 aziende che investono in comunicazione. Dopo cinque anni consecutivi di crescita a doppia cifra, il settore entra in una fase di consolidamento: il 95% delle imprese intervistate ha investito in eventi nell’ultimo anno e quasi tre su dieci hanno destinato al comparto oltre un quinto del proprio budget di comunicazione. Una percentuale che sale al 55% tra le realtà con maggiori investimenti. «Quello degli eventi è un comparto industriale che genera opportunità per un’intera filiera di imprese, professionisti e territori», afferma Salvatore Sagone, presidente e cofondatore di ADC Group. Al centro del confronto veneziano le nuove frontiere della creatività, l’evoluzione dei linguaggi e la capacità di generare esperienze memorabili. «Gli eventi, grazie alla partecipazione fisica, garantiscono un rapporto autentico e diretto tra brand e consumatori», precisa Sagone. Una sfida che investe l’intero ecosistema della comunicazione: trasformare il tempo trascorso insieme in valore economico, reputazionale e relazionale.

La via italiana

L’Italia cresce, ma rischia di perdere pezzi di mercato a vantaggio delle destinazioni internazionali. Negli ultimi due anni il 79% delle aziende intervistate ha rinunciato a realizzare un evento o ha deciso di spostarlo per ragioni legate a costi, regole e burocrazia. Il 38,7% ha scelto una destinazione estera, percentuale che sale al 46,3% tra le imprese industriali e al 50,6% tra quelle con i maggiori budget di comunicazione. «I dati dimostrano che esiste ancora un significativo potenziale di crescita, ma per esprimerlo pienamente è necessario creare condizioni favorevoli agli investimenti, semplificare le procedure e rafforzare la competitività dell’Italia rispetto alle destinazioni internazionali», dice Sagone. Intanto il 17,5% delle imprese prevede di ridurre il peso degli eventi sul proprio budget nei prossimi due anni, contro il 4% rilevato nel 2025. Una prudenza che riguarda soprattutto le aziende più piccole. Cambiano anche i format: crescono i lanci di prodotti e servizi, le inaugurazioni e le attività di team building. Si investe in modo più selettivo, privilegiando iniziative legate a obiettivi aziendali concreti.

AI e capitale relazionale

Non più soltanto il ritorno sull’investimento, ma anche il ritorno sulla relazione. È uno dei cambiamenti più significativi che stanno attraversando l’industria degli eventi. Secondo l’European Experience Index 2026, realizzato da 27Names coinvolgendo aziende e agenzie in 27 Paesi europei, la rilevanza attribuita al Return on Relationship (ROR), indicatore del valore delle relazioni generate dagli eventi, passa dal 16% del 2025 al 58% del 2026. Cresce anche la richiesta di esperienze personalizzate dal 37% al 59%. Una trasformazione che avviene in uno scenario europeo caratterizzato da maggiore prudenza: soltanto il 34% dei budget destinati agli eventi registra un incremento, mentre il restante 66% rimane stabile o diminuisce. Intanto in Italia il 79,1% delle aziende che investono o intendono investire in eventi utilizza indicatori per valutarne i risultati. L’87% utilizza già l’intelligenza artificiale, soprattutto per la produzione di contenuti (33%), l’analisi dei dati (30,3%) e la personalizzazione delle esperienze (29,4%). Il paradosso di questa stagione della comunicazione è che proprio mentre avanza l’automazione, acquista centralità la dimensione umana. In fondo non basta più raggiungere un pubblico. Ora si ha la consapevolezza che bisogna costruire con quel pubblico una relazione destinata a durare.
