articles.title: Perfil | Hernández de Cos, un liberal pragmático experto en forjar consensos
articles.summary: El próximo presidente del BCE, después de tres décadas en bancos centrales, asumirá un desafío mayúsculo: una potencial crisis en Francia
articles.preview: El próximo presidente del BCE, después de tres décadas en bancos centrales, asumirá un desafío mayúsculo: una potencial crisis en Francia Los banqueros centrales tienen un aire a los personajes de Raymond Carver. Pasar, lo que se dice pasar, no les pasa casi nada, pero el lector está todo el tiempo inquieto porque intuye que, por detrás, de alguna forma, en algún lugar, algo —una sacudida, quizá una desgracia— está a punto de ocurrirles.
articles.body:
El próximo presidente del BCE, después de tres décadas en bancos centrales, asumirá un desafío mayúsculo: una potencial crisis en Francia

Los banqueros centrales tienen un aire a los personajes de Raymond Carver. Pasar, lo que se dice pasar, no les pasa casi nada, pero el lector está todo el tiempo inquieto porque intuye que, por detrás, de alguna forma, en algún lugar, algo —una sacudida, quizá una desgracia— está a punto de ocurrirles. Ese trabajo que la mayoría de la gente no entiende y que muchos consideran algo siniestro consiste la mayor parte del tiempo en que parezca que la mona se vista de seda. Hasta que de repente la economía o los mercados pisan una gigantesca piel de plátano, y esos personajes de Carver abren los noticieros y la vida se llena de oscuras espirales y tangentes. Pablo Hernández de Cos (Madrid, 55 años) es un tipo discreto, afable, de trato exquisito, perennemente vestido con un traje azul bien planchado, una corbata prudente y unos zapatos que siempre parecen saber a dónde ir: perfecto para un cuento de Carver. Va a convertirse en presidente del BCE, tal vez el puesto con más poder ejecutivo que ha tenido un español en la escena económica internacional. Y si el lector, a estas alturas, está inquieto porque intuye que algo está a punto de ocurrir, está en lo cierto: De Cos ha sido nombrado a apenas unos días de las elecciones españolas, y asumirá el cargo a apenas unas semanas de las elecciones francesas, y para entonces es muy posible que desde el primer día tenga que enfrentarse a situaciones de enorme tensión. Porque la economía europea languidece. Porque la geopolítica está patas arriba. Porque en teoría los bancos centrales están libres de interferencias políticas, pero con la marea ultra esa frase hace aguas. Porque la inflación se ha ido al 4% tras el shock energético provocado por las guerras. Y sobre todo por Francia.

Francia aparece en algunos cuentos de Carver y ese país, sumido en un mar de crisis, va a tener un papel decisivo en la trayectoria de nuestro antihéroe. La economía francesa va camino de la recesión. Tiene un presidente pato cojo que ha cambiado media docena de veces de primer ministro y que ha resultado ser un bluf. Hay lío en las calles de las grandes ciudades, con una ciudadanía que sabe protestar como ninguna otra. Tiene todos los números para una crisis fiscal en ciernes, con el déficit del 6% del PIB, la deuda del 120%, la prima de riesgo en cotas de aquella crisis del euro de hace 15 años, y todo eso sin presupuesto. Y sobre todo guarda en la recámara a dos candidatos a presidir la República, Marine Le Pen y Jean Luc Mélenchon, con propuestas extravagantes. Francia está abocada a un ajuste fiscal. Si es por las buenas y lo decide el próximo Gobierno, es probable que veamos volar adoquines por París. Y si es por las malas, con los vigilantes del mercado de bonos enfurecidos, los telediarios abrirán con ese personaje de Carver que se estará jugando el mostacho y la credibilidad de la institución que salvó una pelota de partido hace tres lustros, con Draghi al frente. Si de veras viene otra pelota de partido, los belgas, los italianos y los españoles tendrán que poner las barbas a remojar. Y De Cos tendrá mucho, mucho trabajo.

Pablo Hernández de Cos nace en Madrid en los estertores del franquismo, y crece en un barrio de clase media, Hortaleza, y con un padre que le marca tanto como suelen marcar las figuras paternas en la literatura americana: es el secretario de Adolfo Suárez, su hombre de confianza, su inseparable sombra durante años. Estudia Económicas y Derecho. Se casa con una psicóloga que tiene una importancia crucial de puertas adentro —la tentación de la metáfora, de nuevo—, y con quien tiene dos hijas. Y no quiere ser otra cosa en toda su vida que banquero central en uno de esos edificios que parecen un cruce entre el Hogwarts de Harry Potter, la Estrella de la Muerte de La Guerra de las Galaxias y el despacho de Scrooge en el Cuento de Navidad de Dickens. Al lado del suyo en el Banco de España había un par de cuadros de Goya y la colección completa de The Economist desde el siglo XIX, con una de esas historias maravillosas que esconden las viejas bibliotecas y que De Cos contaba maravillosamente.

Estos perfiles suelen ser más atractivos cuando incluyen un par de anécdotas jugosas. En medio de la crisis del euro, este humilde gacetillero asistió a una conversación con mucho picante entre De Cos, Draghi y Ben Bernanke en Sintra, Portugal, que bien podría valer para ese empeño, pero prefiere otras dos estampas que cuentan dos de sus más estrechos colaboradores. Con apenas 25 años, Hernández de Cos ingresa en el Banco de España y una de sus primeras tareas es discutir en público un trabajo de José Manuel González Páramo, una de las figuras totémicas de la institución. “Un marrón en toda regla: un júnior contra un gigante”, describe otro amigo suyo. No se arredra: con la máxima educación, cuestiona ese trabajo y acaba encandilando a González Páramo, que dirigirá su tesis doctoral y se lo llevará más adelante a Fráncfort. Al final de la era Zapatero, y en otra de esas reuniones con mandamases, el gobernador Miguel Fernández Ordóñez pide ideas sobre una futura reforma laboral, una de sus obsesiones. Lejos de quedarse con los séniors, Fernández Ordóñez se decanta por el análisis de un joven jurista, Félix Bolaños, que después acabará como uno de los ministros con más peso en el Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez, y el de un joven economista: Pablo Hernández de Cos. Esas dos historias reflejan un puñado de atributos del flamante presidente del BCE: una gran capacidad de trabajo y una todavía mejor capacidad de análisis, unida a ciertas dotes de seducción que le convierten en lo que los anglosajones denominan un player, alguien que sabe moverse entre bambalinas y politiquear para armar mayorías sólidas.

De Cos es un liberal moderado. Cree que la economía funciona cuando lo hacen sus instituciones básicas, incluidos los mercados. Es un ortodoxo: sin eso nunca habría llegado a la sede de la calle Alcalá, ni mucho menos a la de Fráncfort. Pero no es un liberalón acartonado: está convencido de que el Estado y las políticas fiscales juegan un papel fundamental en ese castillo de naipes con forma de sistema que a cada tanto se nos cae de las manos. De Cos, en fin, es un centrista nato: un mediocentro organizador (y del Atleti, nada menos). A veces demasiado centrista: algunas de sus críticas en los últimos años tienen fuste, como sus disputas con José Luis Escrivá por la reforma de pensiones, pero en otras sus planteamientos han chocado con la cruda realidad, como su rechazo a las subidas del salario mínimo interprofesional, que no tuvieron las consecuencias nefastas que él vaticinaba. Hizo buenas migas con los ministros económicos del PP, e incluso llegó a sonar como ministro de Feijóo hace unos años, cuando Feijóo no quiso ser presidente. Y también mantuvo buenas relaciones con los del Gobierno de Sánchez (incluida Yolanda Díaz), con la excepción de Nadia Calviño y Escrivá. “Lleva toda la vida preparándose para el BCE”, dice de él un ex alto cargo del Banco de España. “Con esa trayectoria, es el más tecnócrata de quienes han llegado a presidir el Eurobanco”, coinciden fuentes de Fráncfort.

Nombrado como gobernador por Román Escolano en los estertores de la era Rajoy, hasta sus detractores, que también los hay, admiten que siempre ha estado donde tenía que estar: supo poner el Banco de España en su sitio después de una temporada de turbulencias, y se ganó a Draghi (que le puso la cruz a su competidor, el holandés Klaas Knot: Draghi es mal enemigo) y a Christine Lagarde. Ha demostrado que domina el difícil arte de forjar consensos, tal vez el principal atributo necesario para encajar en su nuevo puesto tras su fugaz paso por el Banco Internacional de Pagos. “Pero no tiene experiencia en la gestión de crisis graves, y ese es en el fondo su nuevo trabajo”, señalan fuentes financieras como aviso a navegantes.

Quienes le conocen apuntan que intentará ser un híbrido de Draghi, en el estilo y la forma de comunicar de puertas afuera, y de Lagarde de puertas adentro, usando sus habilidades políticas para hacerse con el consejo. “Dicen que es el más duro, el más halcón del Sur, pero en las circunstancias actuales, con un shock de oferta y la incertidumbre en máximos, esa distinción entre halcones y palomas no tiene sentido. Es un banquero central capaz y respetado. Pero tiene ante sí un trabajo realmente difícil porque Francia representa un riesgo existencial equivalente a aquella crisis que solo acabó con el whatever it takes de Draghi”, apunta Alessandro Merli, de la Johns Hopkins.

Entre los libros de Carver el título que más encaja con el horizonte que le espera es Short cuts, o quizá Bajo una luz marina, muy adecuado para un cuadro de Vermeer, una de sus grandes pasiones, con esa luz agónica, macilenta, tan holandesa, tan de estos días locos. Le espera en Fráncfort su trabajo soñado, aunque quizá no contaba con un arranque tan inquietante como los de un cuento de Carver: para explicar lo frágil que puede ser el punto de partida de una historia que sin embargo uno sabe que le importará mucho escribir, el escritor estadounidense ponía el ejemplo de la primera frase de una de las suyas: “Estaba pasando la aspiradora cuando sonó el teléfono”. A ver qué diantre sucede en su nuevo despacho después de ese timbrazo. En uno de sus últimos discursos deja las cosas claras: “Si el mal funcionamiento de los mercados amenaza la estabilidad financiera o la transmisión de la política monetaria, los bancos centrales deben intervenir”. Cuando suene el teléfono habrá que acordarse de esa frase.

articles.summary: El exgobernador del Banco de España relevará a Lagarde al frente de la autoridad monetaria europea tras obtener el apoyo de Francia y Alemania
articles.preview: El economista madrileño Pablo Hernández de Cos se convertirá a partir del 8 de febrero en el presidente del Banco Central Europeo (BCE). El exgobernador del Banco de España relevará a Christine Lagarde, que deja el puesto nueve meses antes de que culmine su mandato, y será el primer español en ocupar el sillón presidencial desde que se fundó la máxima autoridad monetaria de la eurozona en 1998, y la quinta persona en desempeñar este papel.
articles.body:
El economista madrileño Pablo Hernández de Cos se convertirá a partir del 8 de febrero en el presidente del Banco Central Europeo (BCE). El exgobernador del Banco de España relevará a Christine Lagarde, que deja el puesto nueve meses antes de que culmine su mandato, y será el primer español en ocupar el sillón presidencial desde que se fundó la máxima autoridad monetaria de la eurozona en 1998, y la quinta persona en desempeñar este papel.

Se ha impuesto al otro aspirante al cargo, el holandés Klaas Knot, otro exgobernador del banco central de su país, que ha mantenido el pulso hasta el final. España suma así poder en la UE, donde Nadia Calviño preside el Banco Europeo de Inversiones (BEI) y Teresa Ribera ocupa el cargo de número dos de la Comisión Europea. Hernández de Cos, hoy presidente del Banco Internacional de Pagos, ha recabado el consenso necesario en la zona euro y el apoyo clave de Berlín y París, principales accionistas de la institución financiera y el eje que moviliza la UE.

articles.title: Crescono i consumi fuoricasa. La filiera si prepara per Host 2027
articles.summary: Presentato l’Osservatorio HostMilano: industria da 243 miliardi di euro. Macchine per gelati, panificazione e pasticceria trainano il mercato
articles.preview: Presentato l’Osservatorio HostMilano: industria da 243 miliardi di euro. Macchine per gelati, panificazione e pasticceria trainano il mercato Se c’è un settore che sembra non conoscere crisi, nonostante il calo generale dei consumi e la perdita di potere d’acquisto dei salari, è quello dei consumi fuoricasa, in particolare legati alla ristorazione e all’ospitalità.
articles.body:
Presentato l’Osservatorio HostMilano: industria da 243 miliardi di euro. Macchine per gelati, panificazione e pasticceria trainano il mercato

Se c’è un settore che sembra non conoscere crisi, nonostante il calo generale dei consumi e la perdita di potere d’acquisto dei salari, è quello dei consumi fuoricasa, in particolare legati alla ristorazione e all’ospitalità.

Lo confermano i numeri elaborati da ExportPlanning per l’Osservatorio HostMilano, in occasione del lancio della 45esima edizione della kermesse di Fiera Milano, dedicata alla filiera dell’ospitalità professionale, del fuoricasa e del food retail, che si terrà dal 22 al 26 ottobre 2027. Sono già 1.200 gli espositori iscritti, di cui 604 italiani e 640 internazionali, in arrivo da 53 Paesi, con Germania, Spagna, Francia, Stati Uniti e Portogallo tra i Paesi più rappresentati.

Gelati, pane e dolci trainano il mercato

La produzione mondiale della filiera ha infatti superato i 243 miliardi di euro nel 2025, mentre il commercio internazionale ha raggiunto i 175,4 miliardi e, dopo una crescita attesa attorno all’1,2% per quest’anno, gli scambi dovrebbero incrementare del 4,7% nel 2027, per superare i 210 miliardi di euro nel 2030.

A trainare il comparto, si legge nell’Osservatorio, sono i segmenti più legati ai nuovi format del fuoricasa: nel 2026 il commercio mondiale di macchine per gelato e refrigerazione è stimato in crescita del 13,7%, quello di macchine per panificazione e pasticceria + 4,1% e quello di macchine da caffè e vending +3,7%. Solida anche la posizione dell’Italia, che nel 2025 ha espresso una produzione di 12,2 miliardi di euro ed esportazioni per oltre 8,7 miliardi.

Per questa’anno, ExportPlanning stima una crescita dell’export del 2,6%, con un incremento dell’8,8% per le macchine per panificazione e pasticceria, e prevede che le vendite all’estero raggiungano i 9,8 miliardi di euro nel 2030, mentre il saldo commerciale del comparto, atteso a 4,9 miliardi nel 2026, salirà a 5,1 miliardi.

articles.title: China reserves right to take ‘necessary measures’ after Trump’s new tariff proposals

articles.preview: Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’, while Brazil ‘will not yield to this type of threat’ Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash. Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits.
articles.body:
Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash.

Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. It would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.

“China urges the United States to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” the Chinese commerce ministry spokesman, He Yadong, said at a regular briefing. “China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.”

Brazil was also singled out in the announcement after trade talks stalled.

Brazil’s government said on Wednesday that “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.

It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.

The Trump administration said that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries. They are being imposed under a law that allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base”.

The Trump administration’s new tariff rates would be capped at lower levels agreed under trade deals that have already been concluded or remain under negotiation.

The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.

Trump met his counterpart, Xi Jinping, in Shenzhen last week but the escalation in tariffs will not be a surprise to China, Dan Wang, a director on Eurasia Group’s China team, told AFP news agency.

The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027. Trump and Xi are expected to meet again in Miami on the sidelines of the G20 in December.

“It has become a pattern before every major top leader summit,” Wang said, adding that she did not think the new measures would derail relations between Washington and Beijing.

“Xi has a high incentive to keep bilateral relations stable leading up to the 21st (Communist) party congress in October 2027,”Wang said.

A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was a source of excess capacity.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Trump andd Xi.

Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” said the spokesperson Guo Jiakun.

Greer told CNBC that the administration was proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer said. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”

Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined”, said Derek Scissors, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”

The EU said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected the US to stick by a deal struck last year. “The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” said the European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill.

Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.

It added it was “preparing and submitting rebuttal comments on the preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions and allegations made by interested parties”.

In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in any sector, adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.

Taiwan was also earmarked for new tariffs but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing 15% tariff rate.

Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech products that account for more than 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.

Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, Cambodia, the EU, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland and Thailand.

Tokyo’s top government spokesperson, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.

Singapore’s government said it was “very disappointed” with the proposals and denied it was protecting its domestic market or subsidising manufacturing.

Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will probably support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.

However, the Democratic senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos”.

He added: “This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”

With Associated Press and Reuters

articles.title: Indian trade body urges retaliatory tariffs on US goods, warns 500,000 jobs at risk
articles.summary: More than US$48 billion worth of Indian exports could be affected by the proposed US tariffs, with the textile, gems and jewellery, auto components and seafood industries among the hardest hit, a trade body warns.
articles.preview: More than US$48 billion worth of Indian exports could be affected by the proposed US tariffs, with the textile, gems and jewellery, auto components and seafood industries among the hardest hit, a trade body warns. BENGALURU: An Indian trade body has urged New Delhi to impose retaliatory tariffs of 25 per cent on American goods, warning that Washington's latest tariff proposals could put 500,000 jobs at risk and affect more than US$48 billion worth of Indian exports.
articles.body:
More than US$48 billion worth of Indian exports could be affected by the proposed US tariffs, with the textile, gems and jewellery, auto components and seafood industries among the hardest hit, a trade body warns.

BENGALURU: An Indian trade body has urged New Delhi to impose retaliatory tariffs of 25 per cent on American goods, warning that Washington's latest tariff proposals could put 500,000 jobs at risk and affect more than US$48 billion worth of Indian exports.

Brijesh Goyal, chairman of the Delhi-based Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI), said in a statement shared with CNA on Thursday (Nov 26) that the textile, leather, gems and jewellery, auto components and seafood industries could be severely affected.

The US Trade Representative (USTR) proposed tariffs of up to 25 per cent on Indian goods over allegations that India produces more goods than its market needs, potentially falling to 17 per cent if New Delhi reaches a trade deal with Washington.

India's Commerce Ministry said it was reviewing the US proposal, reiterating that the country had no structural excess manufacturing capacity in any sector and that trade-related concerns should be addressed through ongoing bilateral negotiations.

Before the announcement, Indian goods covered by an earlier US Section 301 measure faced an additional 10 per cent tariff, imposed in July following a separate investigation concerning forced labour, according to India's Commerce Ministry.

The USTR said the proposed tariffs would account for existing Section 301 duties rather than being added on top of them, meaning Indian goods already subject to a 10 per cent additional tariff could face a rate of up to 25 per cent, rather than 35 per cent.

Certain products, including smartphones, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, metals, vehicles and aircraft parts, are exempt from the proposed tariffs, although existing duties may still apply.

Goyal said CTI had written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi urging him to impose matching tariffs on goods from the United States, pointing to imports of American minerals, gems and jewellery, machinery, aircraft equipment, electronics, plastics, chemicals, and iron and steel.

“India should reduce its dependence on America for all these things and look for options in other countries,” Goyal said.

Meanwhile, Chandrima Chatterjee, secretary general of the Confederation of Indian Textile Industry (CITI), warned that frequent tariff changes were creating uncertainty for exporters and overseas buyers, disrupting trade negotiations, pricing and order commitments.

Rohit Kumar, chairman of the India Trade Council, echoed these concerns, and told CNA that prolonged tariff uncertainty was already affecting sourcing decisions by American buyers.

“US buyers are nervous. They are shifting manufacturing to the US as much as possible,” he said, adding that while such a shift was not feasible for many products, it remained a long-term goal.

Kumar argued that other Asian manufacturing hubs, including Vietnam and Bangladesh, were not necessarily safer alternatives to India, as they could face similar tariff actions.

Ajay Srivastava, founder of Indian trade policy think tank Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), described the USTR's proposed tariffs as “a deliberate bait to extract one-sided concessions” in the trade negotiations and urged India to reject such a deal.

The proposed US tariffs have not yet taken effect, with Washington seeking public comments until Jan 5, 2027, ahead of hearings scheduled to begin on Jan 25, according to the USTR.

A hawkish member of the Bank of Japan’s policy board called for early action to keep raising the BOJ’s benchmark rate, supporting market expectations for a rate hike next month.

“I believe that the bank needs to bring the policy rate to the neutral level soon,” Naoki Tamura said Thursday in a speech to local business leaders in Yamanashi, west of Tokyo. A neutral level refers to a level that’s neither restrictive nor stimulative for the economy.

“Given that underlying consumer price inflation in Japan isn’t firmly anchored at our 2% target, I believe the bank is required to respond swiftly to signs of an upward deviation in prices, including through accelerated policy interest rate hikes,” Tamura said.

articles.body:
China urges the United States to return to dialogue after Washington unveils new tariffs of up to 20 per cent, with Beijing reserving the right to respond.

BEIJING: China said on Thursday (Nov 26) it reserves the right to take "necessary measures" after Washington unveiled new tariffs that could shake the uneasy truce in the two economic giants' trade war.

Chinese commerce ministry spokesman He Yadong told a regular briefing that citing "overcapacity" as a reason to impose tariffs was a "pretext for protectionism".

"Such actions not only fail to address their own structural imbalances but also disrupt the security and stability of global industrial and supply chains, hinder industrial cooperation, drive up global inflation, harm the direct interests of businesses and consumers and pose long-term, systemic risks to global economic growth," He said.

"China urges the United States to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation," He added.

"China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests."

US President Donald Trump has long criticised China's yawning trade surplus with the United States, which he has blamed for a decline in local manufacturing prowess and jobs.

After starting a second term in office last year, Trump imposed new tariffs on Chinese goods, kicking off a tit-for-tat escalation that at one point saw duties touch 145 per cent.

The trade ceasefire struck by Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in October 2025 is due to expire in January, after a two-month extension was agreed in September.

Th two men met last week at an APEC summit in Shenzhen in southern China and are due to see each other for the fourth time this year in December at a G20 summit in the United States.

The proposed new US levies target a range of trading partners including China, the European Union and Japan and range up to 20 per cent.

China is among those facing the highest 20-per cent rate, but US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing.

"China understands that we're going to have some level of tariffs. This falls within that understanding," he told US broadcaster CNBC, adding that the US was offering China exemptions on around US$30 billion of goods.
